From Bearing Types and Loads

Identify a radial load. A force acts vertically downward on a horizontal shaft. The shaft axis is horizontal. Which load is this?

Choose an answer, then check it.
Show explanation

Answer 1. The force is perpendicular to the shaft axis, so it is radial.

From Bearing Types and Loads

Recognize combined loading. A shaft carries a sideways belt pull and a separate force along its axis. What must its complete support arrangement carry?

Choose an answer, then check it.
Show explanation

Answer 2. The two perpendicular components make combined loading. They may be assigned to different bearings.

From Bearing Types and Loads

Select for repeated starts. A small shaft repeatedly starts and runs at moderate speed under radial load and modest thrust in either direction. Which is a sensible first catalog candidate if low starting resistance matters?

Choose an answer, then check it.
Show explanation

Answer 3. A deep-groove ball bearing can carry radial load and thrust in both directions with generally low starting resistance. Final selection still needs speed, load, life and lubrication checks.

From Bearing Types and Loads

Avoid the plain-bearing speed myth. A continuously running high-speed shaft already has an engineered oil supply. Must all plain bearings be rejected for speed alone?

Choose an answer, then check it.
Show explanation

Answer 2. Fluid-film bearings serve high-speed machinery. Their design and oil conditions matter; the category name is not a speed limit.

From Shaft Support and Axial Adjustment

Find the locating support. Support A retains both rings axially and is rated for radial load and thrust both ways. Support B carries radial load while allowing axial travel. Which end locates the shaft?

Choose an answer, then check it.
Show explanation

Answer 1. A provides axial location and carries the applied thrust. B accommodates relative axial growth.

From Shaft Support and Axial Adjustment

Predict exhausted floating travel. The shaft wants more thermal growth than the floating seat has travel. What happens in the ideal model?

Choose an answer, then check it.
Show explanation

Answer 3. Floating works only while sufficient travel remains. After the limit is reached, the support arrangement resists further expansion.

From Linear Bearing Guides

Count round-shaft freedoms. In the ideal geometric model, an adequately supported round sleeve has no anti-rotation key or axial stop. How many rigid-body freedoms remain? This is not a rotary service rating.

Choose an answer, then check it.
Show explanation

Answer 2. Translation and rotation about the shaft remain: two freedoms. Four are restrained. Ball-bushing rotary service still requires a suitable product rating.

From Linear Bearing Guides

Count profile-guide freedoms. A properly engaged profile carriage supports its rated transverse forces and moments. Which intended motion remains?

Choose an answer, then check it.
Show explanation

Answer 3. The profile geometry restrains the other five ideal rigid-body motions.

From Shaft Support and Axial Adjustment

Choose a rigid spacer. An assembly instruction specifies setting an end-cover position with a measured rigid spacer thickness. Which part performs that job?

Choose an answer, then check it.
Show explanation

Answer 1. A shim sets distance in the stack. The assembly geometry determines how its thickness changes end play.

From Shaft Support and Axial Adjustment

Maintain preload over small movement. An arrangement calls for a specified preload while allowing small dimensional changes. Which approach is appropriate?

Choose an answer, then check it.
Show explanation

Answer 2. A properly selected wave or Belleville spring applies force over a working deflection range. The required preload is a specification, not a feel test.

From Shaft Support and Axial Adjustment

Calculate free shaft growth. A 600 mm carbon-steel shaft warms uniformly by 40 °C and is free to expand. Use ΔL = α·L·ΔT, where L is the original length and ΔT is the temperature rise. For this estimate, use a constant α = 10.44 × 10−6 per °C. How much does the shaft length increase, in mm? Keep at least four significant figures in calculations and report four significant figures.

Enter an answer, then check it.
Show worked solution

The DOE Fundamentals Handbook, Material Science, Volume 2, Table 1 (MS-03, page 2) lists carbon steel at 5.8 × 10−6 per °F. A temperature rise of 1 °C equals a rise of 1.8 °F, so α = 5.8 × 10−6 × 1.8 = 10.44 × 10−6 per °C.

ΔL = (10.44 × 10−6 /°C)(600 mm)(40 °C) = 0.25056 mm ≈ 0.2506 mm. Using mm for L gives mm for ΔL. Four significant figures describe the arithmetic, not the accuracy of this approximate material coefficient.

From Belt, Chain and Gear Drives

1. Synchronize separated shafts: Two separated parallel shafts must stay synchronized in a clean area where oil at the drive contact is unwanted. Which ordinary drive is the best starting candidate? 1 = flat belt; 2 = timing belt; 3 = lubricated roller chain; 4 = a single compact gear pair.

Enter a number, then check it.
Show worked solution

2 — timing belt. Teeth maintain timing and the belt contact runs dry. A flat belt can slip; ordinary chain needs joint lubrication; a compact gear pair cannot bridge the stated gap. This is a shortlist choice, followed by load and environment checks.

From Belt, Chain and Gear Drives

2. Quiet fan drive on a budget: A sheltered fan has separated parallel shafts. Low initial cost and quiet running matter, and a little speed variation is acceptable. Which is the best starting candidate? 1 = V-belt; 2 = precision helical gearbox with extra shafts; 3 = exposed roller chain; 4 = precision timing drive solely to guarantee synchronization.

Enter a number, then check it.
Show worked solution

1 — V-belt. The job accepts the speed variation of a friction drive and benefits from a simple, quiet flexible span. The other choices add requirements or costs the scenario does not call for. Check the actual power and pulley ratings before selection.

From Chain Drives

3. Match an existing chain interface: A sheltered low-speed conveyor has serviceable ANSI #40 sprockets, suitable lubrication access and no requirement for quiet precision positioning. Which replacement transmission fits these specified wheels? 1 = flat belt; 2 = V-belt; 3 = compatible #40 roller chain; 4 = 08B chain chosen only because its pitch is also 12.7 mm.

Enter a number, then check it.
Show worked solution

3 — compatible #40 roller chain. Match chain series and dimensions as well as pitch. Equal pitch alone does not make 08B interchangeable with #40. Confirm the strand count, load rating and connecting-link type too.

From Gear Drives and Tooth Geometry

4. Quieter drive in a compact housing: A compact lubricated gearbox has close parallel shafts and needs smoother high-speed engagement than a comparable spur pair. The bearing arrangement can carry axial thrust. Which candidate best addresses that requirement? 1 = a spur pair selected only for zero axial thrust; 2 = a slipping flat belt; 3 = a long exposed chain; 4 = a matched helical pair.

Enter a number, then check it.
Show worked solution

4 — a matched helical pair. Progressive engagement generally improves smoothness and noise. The stated bearing capability addresses its axial thrust, but the tooth and bearing ratings still need checking.

From Chain Drives

5. Read #25 pitch: What is the nominal pitch of ANSI #25 chain, in inches? Enter a decimal to three places.

Enter a number, then check it.
Show worked solution

Remove the final digit of 25: 2/8 = 0.250 in. The answer is 0.250 in. The final 5 describes bush-chain construction; it does not mean a 5 in pitch.

From Chain Drives

6. Read #35 pitch: What is the nominal pitch of ANSI #35 chain, in inches? Enter a decimal to three places.

Enter a number, then check it.
Show worked solution

Remove the final digit: 3/8 = 0.375 in. The answer is 0.375 in, not 35/8 in and not 0.35 in.

From Chain Drives

7. Read #40-2 pitch: An ANSI #40-2 chain has two parallel strands. What is its nominal pitch in inches? Enter a decimal to three places.

Enter a number, then check it.
Show worked solution

The base number is 40: 4/8 = 0.500 in. The answer is 0.500 in. The -2 changes the strand count, not the pitch.

From Chain Drives

8. Look up 08B pitch: A B-series lookup lists 05B-1 at 8.000 mm, 06B-1 at 9.525 mm, 08B-1 at 12.700 mm and 10B-1 at 15.875 mm. What pitch should a student record for 08B-1, to two decimal places in millimeters?

Enter a number, then check it.
Show worked solution

The 08B-1 row gives 12.70 mm. For this size, 8/16 in is 0.5 in, and 0.5 × 25.4 = 12.70 mm. Do not read 08 as 8 mm, and do not generalize this fraction rule to small sizes such as 05B.

From Chain Drives

9. Write a sprocket reduction: A 22-tooth driver turns a 55-tooth driven sprocket with compatible chain and normal engagement. Write the reduction as X:1, input speed over output speed. Enter only X, to two decimal places.

Enter a number, then check it.
Show worked solution

i = Ndriven/Ndriver = 55/22 = 2.50. The reduction is 2.50:1. Enter 2.50. Reversing the tooth counts gives 0.40, the reciprocal, not this reduction. See Gear Ratios.

From Chain Drives

10. Find driven-sprocket speed: A 21-tooth sprocket at 980 rpm drives a 49-tooth sprocket through correctly engaged chain. What is the average driven speed? Round to the nearest rpm; ignore chordal speed ripple.

Enter a number, then check it.
Show worked solution

nout = 980 × 21/49 = 420 rpm. The answer is 420 rpm. A larger driven sprocket turns slower. The inverse calculation would give about 2287 rpm, which fails that direction check. See Gear Ratios.

From Belt Drives

11. Find timing-pulley speed: A timing belt connects a 28-tooth driver at 1440 rpm to a 60-tooth driven pulley. The belt and pulleys match, with no tooth jumping. What is the output speed, rounded to the nearest rpm?

Enter a number, then check it.
Show worked solution

nout = 1440 × 28/60 = 672 rpm. The answer is 672 rpm. Teeth, not outside pulley diameters, establish this ratio. See Gear Ratios.

From Belt Drives

12. Estimate V-belt output speed: A V-belt driver has an effective diameter of 90 mm and runs at 1680 rpm. The driven sheave has an effective diameter of 210 mm. Estimate output speed to the nearest rpm, explicitly assuming no slip.

Enter a number, then check it.
Show worked solution

nout = 1680 × 90/210 = 720 rpm. The no-slip estimate is 720 rpm. It is not a guarantee of actual friction-belt speed under load. Both dimensions use the same effective-diameter convention. See Gear Ratios.

From Keys, Keyways and Shaft Keyseats

A through hub keyway. A hub has a finished through bore and needs a straight internal keyway. A matching broach set and suitable press are available. Choose the direct method.

  1. End mill a slot on the outside of a shaft.
  2. Use a guided push keyway broach.
  3. Use a Woodruff cutter to make a curved shaft recess.
Enter a number, then check it.
Show reasoning

Option 2. The bushing guides the broach inside the existing bore; the feature is a hub keyway.

From Keys, Keyways and Shaft Keyseats

A keyseat ending within the shaft. A straight flat-bottom shaft keyseat ends before either shaft end. Rounded ends in plan view are allowed. Which tool suits this feature?

  1. An end mill with a permitted entry method.
  2. A conventional through-hole keyway broach and bore bushing.
  3. A drill alone.
Enter a number, then check it.
Show reasoning

Option 1. An end mill can enter and travel along this closed-end slot. Its diameter sets the end radius.

From Broaching

Repeated through hex holes. Many identical parts need a through hex hole. A prepared starting hole, suitable press and dedicated hex hole broach are specified. Which method directly produces the profile?

  1. A round reamer alone.
  2. A Woodruff keyseat cutter.
  3. Conventional internal hole broaching.
Enter a number, then check it.
Show reasoning

Option 3. A dedicated hole broach generates the polygon from its specified starting hole. A keyway broach cuts only a slot, not the entire hex.

From Broaching

Between keyway passes. A multi-pass keyway set calls for one added shim after its first pass. Choose the correct next sequence after that pass is complete.

  1. Add an arbitrary shim while the broach remains loaded.
  2. Remove and clean the broach; insert the specified shim behind it; reinsert, lubricate, check alignment and make the next pass.
  3. Repeat without a shim to obtain the specified extra depth.
Enter a number, then check it.
Show reasoning

Option 2. The shim offsets the tool for the next cut. The prescribed stack belongs behind the broach, and setup checks repeat between passes.

From Broaching

Count first and shimmed passes. Invented planning model: the unshimmed pass reaches 1.0 mm radial depth. Each later pass, with one additional shim increment, adds 0.5 mm. How many total passes reach 2.5 mm? Include the first pass; round a fractional added-pass count upward. These are not tool settings.

Enter a number, then check it.
Show reasoning

1 + ceiling((2.5 − 1.0)/0.5) = 1 + 3 = 4 passes. Depths are 1.0, 1.5, 2.0 and 2.5 mm. Three counts only the added passes; five incorrectly divides the full target by the shim increment.

From Broaching

Round up, then check overshoot. Invented model: the first pass reaches 1.0 mm; each added shim increment gives 0.5 mm more depth on the next pass. What minimum total pass count reaches AT LEAST 2.2 mm? Round upward to a whole pass. This counting answer is not permission to exceed a drawing limit.

Enter a number, then check it.
Show reasoning

1 + ceiling((2.2 − 1.0)/0.5) = 1 + ceiling(2.4) = 4. Three passes reach only 2.0 mm. Four reach 2.5 mm, so this schedule is unsuitable if 2.2 mm is the maximum allowed depth.

From Keys, Keyways and Shaft Keyseats

Equal cross-section dimensions. A parallel key has equal width and height and a uniform section along its working length. Identify it.

  1. Square parallel key.
  2. Rectangular parallel key with unequal width and height.
  3. Woodruff key.
Enter a number, then check it.
Show reasoning

Option 1. Square describes equal width and height in cross-section, not the shape of the key seen from above.

From Keys, Keyways and Shaft Keyseats

Unequal cross-section dimensions. A parallel key has unequal width and height, with no taper along its working length. Identify it.

  1. Woodruff key.
  2. Rectangular parallel key.
  3. Gib-head key.
Enter a number, then check it.
Show reasoning

Option 2. This is the rectangular parallel form; the dimensions alone do not specify the required fit.

From Keys, Keyways and Shaft Keyseats

A disk segment seated in a shaft. A key has a curved bottom that sits in a circular recess cut into the shaft. Identify the key.

  1. Square parallel key.
  2. Gib-head key.
  3. Woodruff key.
Enter a number, then check it.
Show reasoning

Option 3. The Woodruff key is a disk segment with a matching curved shaft seat.

From Keys, Keyways and Shaft Keyseats

A tapered key with a removal head. A tapered key has a projecting head that can be engaged to remove it. Identify the key.

  1. Gib-head key.
  2. Woodruff key.
  3. Headless rectangular parallel key.
Enter a number, then check it.
Show reasoning

Option 1. The gib head supplies a place to engage the key for removal.

From Assembly Files and Mates

Count a free component’s motions

A rigid component floats freely in a three-dimensional assembly. It has no mates, contacts, or fixed state. How many independent degrees of freedom does it have relative to the assembly frame?

Enter a number, then check it.
Show answer and reasoning

6 DOF. Three translations and three rotations: 3 + 3 = 6. Three is the count of axes, not the count of independent rigid-body motions.

From Assembly Files and Mates

Seat a flat plate on a base

A free rigid plate receives one coincident mate between its flat underside and the top plane of a grounded base. No other mates or contact constraints exist. How many DOF remain?

Enter a number, then check it.
Show answer and reasoning

3 DOF. The plate can slide in two directions within the plane and rotate about the plane normal. The mate removes normal translation and two tilting motions: 6 − 3 = 3.

From Assembly Files and Mates

Align a shaft with a bore

A free shaft is mated concentrically to the cylindrical bore of a grounded housing. Rotation is not locked. There are no other mates or contacts. How many DOF remain?

Enter a number, then check it.
Show answer and reasoning

2 DOF. Translation along the common axis and rotation about that axis remain. The axis alignment removes four of the initial six independent motions: 6 − 4 = 2.

From Assembly Files and Mates

Seat the shaft shoulder

A shaft already has a concentric mate to a grounded bore, with rotation unlocked. Add a coincident mate between its shoulder face and a housing end face, both perpendicular to the common axis. No other constraints exist. How many DOF remain?

Enter a number, then check it.
Show answer and reasoning

1 DOF. Concentric alignment left axial slide and spin. Seating the shoulder removes the slide. Rotation about the common axis remains: 2 − 1 = 1.

From Assembly Files and Mates

Lock the remaining rotation

A shaft’s axis and shoulder are located as in the previous type of joint: only rotation about its axis remains. An independent angular constraint now fixes that remaining rotation. How many DOF remain? Assume compatible constraints.

Enter a number, then check it.
Show answer and reasoning

0 DOF. The final independent rotation is removed: 1 − 1 = 0. This is appropriate for a stationary part; a pivot meant to turn should retain that rotation.

From Exploded Views and Bills of Materials

Count component instances

One original teaching pivot assembly
ItemPart numberDescriptionQty per assembly
1PV-110Support1
2PV-210Lever1
3PV-310Pivot pin1
4HW-410Thrust washer2
5HW-510Pin retainer1

How many individual component instances are required for one assembly? Count both washers.

Enter a number, then check it.
Show answer and reasoning

6 components. Add the quantity column: 1 + 1 + 1 + 2 + 1 = 6. Five is the number of distinct rows, not the number of instances.

From Exploded Views and Bills of Materials

Count washers for six assemblies

One original teaching pivot assembly
ItemPart numberDescriptionQty per assembly
1PV-110Support1
2PV-210Lever1
3PV-310Pivot pin1
4HW-410Thrust washer2
5HW-510Pin retainer1

How many HW-410 washers are required for six complete assemblies, with no spares?

Enter a number, then check it.
Show answer and reasoning

12 washers. 2 washers/assembly × 6 assemblies = 12 washers. Item number 4 identifies the row; using 4 × 6 = 24 mistakes an identifier for a quantity.

From Assembly Files and Mates

Choose mates that fully locate a cover

A rigid rectangular cover must be stationary relative to a grounded rectangular housing. Their corresponding bottom, side, and end datum planes are mutually perpendicular and geometrically compatible. Choose A, B, or C and explain.

  • A: Coincident bottom planes only.
  • B: Coincident bottom planes, then a parallel mate between those same planes.
  • C: Coincident bottom, corresponding side, and corresponding end planes.

Self-check: write your reasoning before revealing the explanation. This text is not automatically graded or saved.

Show answer and reasoning

C. Seating the bottom leaves two in-plane slides and one spin. The independent side-plane condition removes one slide and that spin. The end-plane condition removes the last slide. A leaves three DOF. B repeats an orientation already established by coincidence. This answer assumes matching perpendicular datum planes, not arbitrary selections.

From Checking CAD Assemblies

Find the redundant relationship

A shaft has a concentric mate to a grounded housing bore, plus a seated shoulder mate. Which proposed addition repeats an existing geometric condition: A, a parallel relation between those same two axes; or B, an independent constraint fixing the remaining shaft rotation? Explain.


Self-check: write your reasoning before revealing the explanation. This text is not automatically graded or saved.

Show answer and reasoning

A is redundant. Coincident axes are already parallel. B removes the remaining spin; whether it is wanted depends on whether the shaft is meant to rotate. Do not add B merely to remove an under-defined indicator.

Choose a meaningful motion check

Self-check: write your reasoning before revealing the explanation. This text is not automatically graded or saved.

Show answer and reasoning

No. Inspect intermediate positions across the intended range and use appropriate interference or collision checks on the whole connected assembly. Endpoint clearance and a moving preview do not establish clearance everywhere. Self-check: write your reasoning before revealing the explanation. This text is not automatically graded or saved.

B. Confirm the correct component identity before repairing its reference. Save the affected documents and check drawings as well as assemblies. Suppressing the component hides the symptom; substituting an unrelated file can make a model open while describing the wrong design.

m = density × volume = 2.70 g/cm³ × 12.0 cm³ = 32.4 g. Cubic centimeters cancel. Dividing volume by density gives about 4.44 and does not give units of mass.

From Coolant Concentration and Mixing

Restore a lean tank with premix: A hypothetical tank contains 34 L at 4.0%. Bring it to 50 L at an assumed target of 6.0%. What premix concentration is required? Give percent to the nearest 0.01%.

All values are hypothetical; use the actual product data sheet in practice. Assume additive liquid volumes, uniform mixing and no loss. Top-up examples assume serviceable fluid and supplier-approved premix.

Enter a number, then check it.
Show worked solution

A = 50 − 34 = 16 L. P = (50 × 6 − 34 × 4) ÷ 16 = 10.25%. Check: (34 × 4 + 16 × 10.25) ÷ 50 = 6%. Premix at 6% would leave the tank lean.

From Coolant Concentration and Mixing

Enter a number, then check it.
Show worked solution

A = 10 L. P = (50 × 6 − 40 × 7) ÷ 10 = 2.00%. Check: (280 + 20) ÷ 50 = 6%. Plain water would instead leave 5.6%.

From Coolant Concentration and Mixing

Find volume from an available premix: A hypothetical tank has 30 L at 4.0%. An approved teaching premix is 8.0%; the desired tank concentration is 5.0%. The allowed final volume is 45 L. How much premix reaches the target? Give liters to the nearest 0.01 L.

Show worked solution

A = 30 × (5 − 4) ÷ (8 − 5) = 10.00 L. Final volume is 40 L, below the 45 L limit. Concentrate balance: (30 × 4 + 10 × 8) ÷ 40 = 5%.

From Coolant Concentration and Mixing

Measure concentrate for the top-up batch: Prepare 16 L of hypothetical 10.25% premix. How many liters of concentrate are needed? Give liters to the nearest 0.01 L.

Concentrate = 16 × 10.25 ÷ 100 = 1.64 L. Water = 16 − 1.64 = 14.36 L. Put water in first, then add concentrate while mixing.

From Coolant Concentration and Mixing

Convert a water-to-concentrate ratio: A hypothetical mixing instruction says 19 parts water to 1 part concentrate, by volume. What percentage of the final mix is concentrate? Give percent to the nearest 0.01%.

From Coolant Concentration and Mixing

Keep all the parts in the denominator: A hypothetical mixing instruction says 31 parts water to 1 part concentrate, by volume. What percentage of the final mix is concentrate? Give percent to the nearest 0.01%.

All values are hypothetical; use the actual product data sheet in practice. Assume additive liquid volumes, uniform mixing and no loss. Top-up examples assume serviceable fluid and supplier-approved premix.

Enter a number, then check it.
Show worked solution

Total parts = 32. Concentrate percentage = 100 ÷ 32 = 3.125%, or 3.13%. Using 100 ÷ 31 gives about 3.23%; reversing the named ingredients gives 96.875%. Neither is the concentrate fraction requested.

From 3D Printing from CAD

Orient a bar for tension

A straight printed bar will be pulled along its length. Compare printing it standing on its end with printing its length parallel to the bed. Assume the same material and a sound print. Which is the better starting orientation, and why?

Self-check: write a reason before revealing. This response is not automatically graded or saved.

Show reasoning

Start with the length parallel to the bed. Printing upright puts the tension across the interfaces between layers, where separation is often easier. Laying the bar down allows paths within layers to run along its length. Actual strength still depends on material, paths, and bonding; test a representative part.

From Laser Cutting and Engraving from CAD

Separate an outline from a filled mark

An approved sheet must yield a rectangular label with a filled dark symbol on its face. Which operation belongs on the outside boundary, and which belongs on the filled symbol? Should a thin score line automatically use through-cut settings?

Self-check: write a reason before revealing. This response is not automatically graded or saved.

Show reasoning

Use a vector cutting path for the outside boundary and raster engraving for the filled symbol. A vector score follows a path but is intended to mark the surface, so it needs an appropriate scoring setup rather than through-cut settings. Verify the assignments in the job preview.

From Laser Cutting and Engraving from CAD

Compensate an outside width

A rectangular cutout must finish 30.00 mm wide. Assume a constant 0.18 mm kerf centered on the path, with no automatic compensation. What path-to-path width produces that finished outside width? Give millimeters to the nearest 0.01 mm.

Enter a number, then check it.
Show worked solution

Each path moves outward by 0.18 / 2 = 0.09 mm. Across both sides, 30.00 + 2 × 0.09 = 30.18 mm. Subtracting kerf would shrink the part further; adding only half the kerf would compensate only one edge.

From Laser Cutting and Engraving from CAD

Compensate an opening

A rectangular opening must finish 12.00 mm wide. Assume a constant 0.22 mm kerf centered on the path and no automatic compensation. What path-to-path width is needed? Give millimeters to the nearest 0.01 mm.

Enter a number, then check it.
Show worked solution

The waste is inside the opening. Move each path inward by 0.22 / 2 = 0.11 mm. The path width is 12.00 − 0.22 = 11.78 mm. Cutting removes half the kerf beyond each path and brings the finished opening back to 12.00 mm.

From Choosing a Fabrication Process

Choose a process for two shapes

Choose an initial process for (A) a flat cover of constant thickness with surface lettering and (B) a one-piece rounded grip whose cross section changes along its length. Approved sheet and printable materials both meet the stated service requirements. Explain a limitation of each choice.

Self-check: write a reason before revealing. This response is not automatically graded or saved.

Show reasoning

A: laser-cut and engrave the sheet; account for kerf, available thickness, and edge quality. B: print the grip; choose orientation for load and surface quality and check support access. A laser could make a grip from stacked profiles, but that changes the one-piece construction requirement. Neither process is automatically faster without estimating the actual jobs.

From Choosing a Fabrication Process

Separate slot clearance from kerf

A measured sheet edge is 3.02 mm thick. Its receiving slot needs 0.10 mm total clearance across the width. Assume a constant 0.20 mm kerf centered on the path and no automatic compensation. What path-to-path slot width produces the desired finished slot? Give millimeters to the nearest 0.01 mm. These are exercise values, not a recommended fit.

Enter a number, then check it.
Show worked solution

First choose the finished opening: 3.02 + 0.10 = 3.12 mm. Then compensate the opening's kerf: 3.12 − 0.20 = 2.92 mm. The cut enlarges this path width to 3.12 mm. Clearance is added once because the question gives total clearance, not clearance per side.

See Laser Cutting and Engraving from CAD for the path-offset method.

6 dimensions: body length, height and thickness (3); hole diameter (1); and two center coordinates (2). THRU states the end condition. This count is for the stated ideal geometry, not a universal count for every production drawing.

8 dimensions: 3 for the body + 1 shared diameter + 2 coordinates for each of 2 centers = 8. A 2X note shares the size; it does not share the center location.

Reason about thread percentage. Two holes will receive the same cutting tap. Within the permitted hole-size range, what generally happens when the prepared hole diameter increases?

Thread height decreases and tapping torque generally decreases. The larger hole leaves less material for the tap to cut. Engagement length is an axial distance and is a separate design choice; thread percentage is not a strength percentage.

From DC Motor Torque, Speed, and Power

Speed at constant load: Assume a fixed-voltage linear torque-speed curve with stall torque 0.8 N·m and no-load speed 3,000 rpm. What steady speed results at a constant resisting load of 0.2 N·m? Give whole rpm.

Enter a number, then check it.
Show worked solution

n = 3,000(1 − 0.2/0.8) = 2,250 rpm. One-quarter stall torque leaves three-quarters no-load speed.

From DC Motor Torque, Speed, and Power

Power at the load point: Assume a fixed-voltage linear torque-speed curve with stall torque 0.8 N·m and no-load speed 3,000 rpm. Find mechanical output power at a constant 0.2 N·m load. Give watts to two decimal places; carry intermediate values to at least four significant figures.

Enter a number, then check it.
Show worked solution

n = 3,000(1 − 0.2/0.8) = 2,250 rpm. ω = 2,250 × 2π/60 = 235.619… rad/s. P = 0.2 × 235.619… = 47.12 W. Using 235.6 rad/s also gives 47.12 W. Multiplying torque by rpm directly gives 450, which is not watts.

From DC Motor Torque, Speed, and Power

Speed of peak power: An ideal linear motor curve has 1.2 N·m stall torque and 3,600 rpm no-load speed. At what speed is shaft output power greatest? Give whole rpm.

Enter a number, then check it.
Show worked solution

Peak power occurs at half no-load speed: 3,600/2 = 1,800 rpm. At 3,600 rpm the external torque is zero, so shaft output power is zero.

From DC Motor Torque, Speed, and Power

Maximum shaft power: An ideal linear motor curve has 1.2 N·m stall torque and 3,600 rpm no-load speed. What is its maximum mechanical output power? Give watts to one decimal place; carry intermediate values to at least four significant figures.

Enter a number, then check it.
Show worked solution

At half speed and half torque: n = 1,800 rpm and T = 0.6 N·m. P = 0.6 × (1,800 × 2π/60) = 113.097… = 113.1 W. Stall torque × no-load angular speed would give 452.4 W: those endpoints cannot occur together.

From Current, Voltage, and Resistance

1. Current in a control circuit: A resistor in a control circuit is 470 Ω. What current flows when 24 V is applied across it? Give the answer in milliamperes.

Enter a number, then check it.
Show worked solution
  1. Pick the form with the two quantities you have: I = V/R = 24 V ÷ 470 Ω = 0.051064 A.

Then move the prefix:

0.051064 A × 1,000 mA1 A = 51.06 mA

The current is 51.1 mA. Check the units rather than trusting the arithmetic: an ohm is a volt per ampere, so volts divided by ohms leaves amperes. And mind the case — mA is a milliampere, while MA would be a megaampere, a billion times larger.

From Current, Voltage, and Resistance

2. Voltage drop along a cord: A portable tool draws 12 A through an extension cord. Both of the cord’s conductors are in the current path — out to the tool and back — and together they add 0.32 Ω to the circuit. What is the voltage drop across the cord?

Enter a number, then check it.
Show worked solution
  1. V = IR = 12 A × 0.32 Ω = 3.84 V.

The drop is 3.84 V, and that is 3.84 V that never reaches the tool: the supply is divided between the cord and the load, and the cord takes its share first.

Read the resistance figure carefully before using it. A cord carries the current out on one conductor and back on the other, so what belongs in this calculation is the resistance of the whole path. A table that gives resistance per unit length gives it for a single conductor; use that figure alone for a cord and the answer comes out about half of what a meter across the ends would show.

From Current, Voltage, and Resistance

3. Resistance from a nameplate: A resistive heating element is rated 1,500 W at 120 V. What resistance does that rating imply?

Enter a number, then check it.
Show worked solution
  1. The two quantities given are power and voltage, so use R = V2/P.
  2. R = (120 V)2 ÷ 1,500 W = 14,400 ÷ 1,500 = 9.6 Ω.

The rating implies 9.6 Ω. Two steps get to the same place if you prefer: I = P/V = 12.5 A, then R = V/I = 120 ÷ 12.5 = 9.6 Ω.

This is the resistance at the rated operating point. A metal heating element is not the same resistance cold as it is hot, so a meter reading on an unpowered element will not match the nameplate figure exactly.

From Current, Voltage, and Resistance

4. Heat lost in a cable run: A cable run carries 25 A and has a total resistance of 0.18 Ω. How much power is lost as heat in it?

Enter a number, then check it.
Show worked solution
  1. P = I2R = (25 A)2 × 0.18 Ω = 625 × 0.18 = 112.5 W.

The run loses 112.5 W as heat, spread along its whole length.

Notice the squared current. Halve the load to 12.5 A and the loss does not halve, it quarters, to 28.1 W. That is why a drop that is harmless on a light load becomes a real problem on a heavy one, and why the length and size of a conductor matter more the more current the load draws.

Each blank consumes 102 mm. Nine consume 918 mm; ten need 1,020 mm and will not fit. Answer: 9 blanks. There are 82 mm left over, plus 18 mm lost to nine kerfs. Ignoring kerf incorrectly predicts ten blanks.

From Material Utilization and Cost

Enter an answer, then check it.
Show worked solution

Useful length = 9 × 110 = 990 mm. Utilization = 990/1,020 × 100 = 97.0588…%, or 97.1%. 1,020 − 9 × 110 = 30 mm of the bar lies outside the finished blanks (kerf plus offcut together).

From Metal Stock Forms and Purchasing

Calculate solid round bar mass: A hypothetical stock estimate specifies density = 2,700 kg/m³. Use that supplied assumption, not a certified alloy property. A solid round bar has diameter 20 mm and length 500 mm. Find its mass in kg, rounded to three decimal places.

Enter a number, then check it.
Show answer and reasoning

Radius = 0.010 m and length = 0.500 m. Volume = π × 0.010² × 0.500 = 0.000157080 m³. Mass = volume × 2,700 = 0.424115 kg, or 0.424 kg. Using the diameter as the radius gives 1.69646 kg, four times too much. This is mass, not weight force.

From Metal Stock Forms and Purchasing

Calculate tube material volume: Round tube has outside diameter 30 mm, wall thickness 3 mm and length 200 mm. Find the volume of metal in cm³, rounded to two decimal places. Ignore end features and manufacturing tolerances.

Enter a number, then check it.
Show answer and reasoning

Inside diameter = 30 − 2 × 3 = 24 mm. Volume = π(30² − 24²) × 200 / 4 = 50,893.801 mm³. Divide by 1,000 to obtain 50.89 cm³. Treating the tube as solid gives 141.37 cm³; subtracting only one wall gives 26.86 cm³.

Enter a number, then check it.
Show worked solution

T = 1/490 s × 1000 = 2.041 ms. Frequency is cycles per second; period is seconds per cycle.

From Pulse-Width Modulation

PWM on-time: An ideal PWM signal is 490 Hz with 25% duty. Find its on-time in microseconds. Keep at least four significant figures in intermediate results.

Enter a number, then check it.
Show worked solution

T = 1/490 = 0.002040816 s. On-time = 0.25 × T × 1000000 = 510.2 µs. Using a rounded T of 2.041 ms gives 510.25 µs.

From Pulse-Width Modulation

Average PWM voltage: An ideal output switches between 0 and 5.000 V at 35% duty. What is its average voltage?

Enter a number, then check it.
Show worked solution

D = 35/100 = 0.35. Average = 0.35 × 5 = 1.750 V. The pin is not steadily at that voltage.

From Pulse-Width Modulation

Nominal analogWrite value: Use the nominal mapping round(255 × D). What analogWrite value requests 35% duty on an Uno R3 PWM pin? Round to the nearest integer.

Enter a number, then check it.
Show worked solution

round(255 × 0.35) = round(89.25) = 89. This is a nominal request, not an exact timer-duty guarantee.

From Milling Vises and Strap Clamps

Higher reading at the right end. The indicator body is on the operator side of the fixed jaw. You verified that moving the jaw toward the body increases the reading. The left mounting point is the pivot; only the right end is adjusted. A left-to-right sweep reads 0.00 mm at the left and +0.08 mm at the right. Which way should the first small correction move the right end?

  1. Toward the indicator.
  2. Away from the indicator.
  3. Along the jaw toward the left end.
Enter a number, then check it.
Show reasoning

Option 2. The right end is closer to the indicator than the left. Move it away, then repeat the sweep and recheck after final tightening. The sign is defined by the response test, not a remembered clockwise dial rule.

From Milling Vises and Strap Clamps

Lower reading at the right end. The indicator body is on the operator side of the fixed jaw. You verified that moving the jaw toward the body increases the reading. The left mounting point is the pivot; only the right end is adjusted. The left reading is +0.02 mm and the right reading is −0.03 mm. Choose the correction.

  1. Move the right end toward the indicator.
  2. Move the right end away from the indicator.
  3. Accept it because neither reading is large.
Enter a number, then check it.
Show reasoning

Option 1. Right minus left is −0.03 − 0.02 = −0.05 mm. The right end is farther from the indicator. Bring it toward the indicator and resweep. Alignment is judged against the specified job tolerance, which this problem does not supply.

From Milling Vises and Strap Clamps

Reversed indicator response. The left mounting point is the pivot. In this new indicator arrangement you verify that moving the jaw toward the body makes the reading DECREASE. Left reads 0.00 mm; right reads +0.04 mm. Which correction should move the right end?

  1. Away from the indicator body.
  2. No correction can be inferred.
  3. Toward the indicator body.
Enter a number, then check it.
Show reasoning

Option 3. With this reversed response, the positive change means the right end is farther away. Move it toward the body. You have enough information because the response was demonstrated; reversing the contact arrangement invalidates a memorized sign rule.

From Milling Vises and Strap Clamps

A jump halfway across the jaw. The indicator body is on the operator side of the fixed jaw. You verified that moving the jaw toward the body increases the reading. The left mounting point is the pivot; only the right end is adjusted. The reading starts at 0.00 mm, rises abruptly to +0.12 mm at one small spot, returns to 0.00 mm and stays there to the far end. What is the best next action?

  1. Tap the right end away until the +0.12 mm spot reads zero.
  2. Inspect and clean the local contact surface and check indicator stability.
  3. Accept the setup without checking the middle.
Enter a number, then check it.
Show reasoning

Option 2. A local jump is not the smooth trend expected from simple jaw rotation. Check for debris, damage or unstable contact, then repeat the entire sweep. Equal endpoints alone do not explain the jump.

From Milling Vises and Strap Clamps

Stud near the part. A strap receives P = 7,200 N. The part-contact-to-stud distance a is 18 mm; the stud-to-heel distance b is 54 mm. What downward force does the strap apply to the part? Assume an ideal weightless strap with only part and heel contacts and a vertical stud load. Round to the nearest newton.

Enter a number, then check it.
Show reasoning

Fpart = P × b / (a + b) = 7,200 × 54 / (18 + 54) = 5,400 N. The heel receives 1,800 N. The two shares sum to 7,200 N. Using a in the numerator gives the heel share, not the requested part share.

From Milling Vises and Strap Clamps

Stud near the heel. A strap receives P = 7,200 N. The part-contact-to-stud distance a is 54 mm; the stud-to-heel distance b is 18 mm. What downward force does the strap apply to the part? Assume an ideal weightless strap with only part and heel contacts and a vertical stud load. Round to the nearest newton.

Enter a number, then check it.
Show reasoning

Fpart = P × b / (a + b) = 7,200 × 18 / (54 + 18) = 1,800 N. The heel receives 5,400 N. The two shares sum to 7,200 N. Using a in the numerator gives the heel share, not the requested part share.

From Milling Vises and Strap Clamps

Unequal clamp arms. A strap receives P = 5,200 N. The part-contact-to-stud distance a is 27 mm; the stud-to-heel distance b is 63 mm. What downward force does the strap apply to the part? Assume an ideal weightless strap with only part and heel contacts and a vertical stud load. Round to the nearest newton.

Enter a number, then check it.
Show reasoning

Fpart = P × b / (a + b) = 5,200 × 63 / (27 + 63) = 3,640 N. The heel receives 1,560 N. The two shares sum to 5,200 N. Using a in the numerator gives the heel share, not the requested part share.

From Milling Vises and Strap Clamps

Clamp-force rounding. A strap receives P = 4,100 N. The part-contact-to-stud distance a is 23 mm; the stud-to-heel distance b is 48 mm. What downward force does the strap apply to the part? Assume an ideal weightless strap with only part and heel contacts and a vertical stud load. Round to the nearest newton.

Enter a number, then check it.
Show reasoning

Fpart = P × b / (a + b) = 4,100 × 48 / (23 + 48) = 2,772 N. The heel receives 1,328 N. The two shares sum to 4,100 N. Using a in the numerator gives the heel share, not the requested part share.

When HSS is a reasonable choice. A modest-speed machine will make a light interrupted cut. The fixture is secure, and the tool maker permits this operation with either listed milling tool. Which reasoning is sound?

From Diagnosing Milling Chatter

Chatter after a longer tool. A formerly clean cut chatters after changing to a much longer end mill. Seating, runout and workholding have been checked. The feature does not need the extra reach. What is the first useful change?

  3. Change speed, feed and depth together so the cause is impossible to isolate.

Show reasoning

Option 1. The changed reach is a clear loss of stiffness. Correct it before tuning around it. Use the shortest reach that still clears the work and holder.

From Diagnosing Milling Chatter

Chatter only inside corners. A correctly seated, rigid setup cuts straight pocket walls cleanly but chatters in tight inside corners. What should you review first?

  1. Whether halving feed everywhere will hide the symptom without changing engagement.
  2. Whether doubling the axial depth will always damp the vibration.

Show reasoning

Option 3. More of the circumference can become engaged in a corner. Smooth or reduce engagement using a suitable path and cutting data, then test the change.

From Diagnosing Milling Chatter

A stable setup at an unstable speed. Seating, rigidity and engagement have been reviewed. Chatter appears at the current speed. Which next experiment is useful?

  1. Always halve feed while leaving speed unchanged.
  2. Try a different permitted spindle speed and review feed to preserve the intended chip load.
  3. Assume that a higher speed can never be stable.

Show reasoning

Option 2. Speed changes the timing of tooth engagement. A different permitted speed may help, but the accompanying feed must still produce a suitable chip load. Slowing feed alone can cause rubbing.

From Diagnosing Milling Chatter

The part lifted during a cut. After ending a noisy cut, you find a gap between the part and one parallel. What takes priority before another trial?

  2. Lower feed until the sound is hidden.

Option 3. A moved part is a setup failure. Restore support and clamping and verify the part reference; do not try to tune speed around it.

From Selecting a Material-Removal Process

Explain a no-HAZ choice

A conductive plate must retain an edge without thermal alteration. Explain why abrasive waterjet is a candidate and why EDM is not automatically a substitute.


Self-check: write first, then compare. Your response is not automatically graded or saved.

Show a model answer

Abrasive waterjet removes by mechanical erosion and normally produces no thermal HAZ. EDM removes by local melting and vaporization, so recast and thermal surface effects remain possible despite low cutting force. Waterjet edge quality and mechanical damage still need evaluation.

From Electrochemical Machining

Distinguish the two liquids

Explain the difference between ECM electrolyte and EDM dielectric, including why “ECM makes no heat” is misleading.


Self-check: write first, then compare. Your response is not automatically graded or saved.

Show a model answer

ECM electrolyte conducts machining current and carries reaction products. EDM dielectric normally insulates until local breakdown permits a discharge, then helps cool and flush the gap. ECM does not melt the work, but current heats the electrolyte.

From Laser, Waterjet and Plasma Cutting

Thickness and finish

A waterjet profile has acceptable dimensions at the top but an unacceptable lower edge. Name two process effects to investigate.


Self-check: write first, then compare. Your response is not automatically graded or saved.

Show a model answer

Check taper (different cut widths through the thickness) and jet lag or striations. Thickness, travel speed and the cutting setup affect both. A no-HAZ process does not guarantee straight walls or the required surface finish.

From Chemical Milling and Etching

Etching a narrow land

Why might a narrow strip of protected metal end up narrower than its mask pattern?


Self-check: write first, then compare. Your response is not automatically graded or saved.

Show a model answer

The etchant can attack sideways beneath the mask edge as well as downward. This undercut must be allowed for in mask design and limits small features, especially for deeper etches.

From Electrical Discharge Machining

Wire center-path offset

For this teaching example, the wire radius is 0.125 mm and the one-sided spark gap is 0.025 mm. What is the offset magnitude from the finished wall to the wire center path? Give mm rounded to the nearest 0.001 mm.

Enter an offset in mm.
Show answer and reasoning

Offset = radius + gap = 0.125 + 0.025 = 0.150 mm. The center path is on the removed-material side of the wall. 0.125 mm ignores the gap; 0.175 mm adds two gaps; 0.275 mm uses the wire diameter. The full kerf is 0.300 mm, not the one-sided offset.

Repeated thermoset parts: A producer needs 40,000 electrical components from a thermosetting molding compound. Both faces need shaped detail, and the charge can spread in matched heated tools. Which process fits?

  2. Rotational molding
  3. Compression molding
  4. Extrusion of thermoplastic pipe
Enter a number, then check it.
Show answer and reasoning

Choice 3: Compression molding. Compression molding presses the charge between matched tools and allows the thermoset to cure. A cooling-only explanation would miss the chemical change.

From Choosing a Plastic Forming Process

Twenty detailed replicas: A designer needs 20 small detailed solid replicas in a casting-grade two-part polyurethane. Flexible molds are available and cure time is acceptable. Which process fits?

  1. Extrusion
  2. Blow molding
  3. Vacuum forming
  4. Casting
Enter a number, then check it.
Show answer and reasoning

Choice 4: Casting. Casting matches the liquid thermosetting resin and short run. Flexible tooling can reproduce detail, but mold life and trapped air still matter.

From Choosing a Plastic Forming Process

Custom reinforced shells: A maker needs eight broad glass-fiber/epoxy equipment covers. One smooth tool-side face is sufficient and manual work is acceptable. Which process fits?

  3. Extrusion
  4. Injection molding of unfilled PP
Enter a number, then check it.
Show answer and reasoning

Choice 2: Wet hand layup. Wet hand layup builds reinforcement and thermosetting resin against a mold. The resulting material belongs to Wood & Composites in the course model. A one-sided mold does not precisely control both faces.

From Plastic Forming Processes

A dimple opposite a thick rib: An injection-molded cover has a shallow depression on the visible face directly opposite a heavy rib. Which design change should be investigated first?

  1. Make every rib as thick as possible.
  2. Reduce the heavy rib or core out the local mass.
  3. Remove all draft so the part stays in place.
Enter a number, then check it.
Show answer and reasoning

Choice 2. The thick region can shrink differently and pull the surface inward, producing sink. Reduce the local mass and check packing and cooling; filling every region thicker is not a general cure.

From Plastic Forming Processes

A part scrapes during ejection: A deep molded wall is parallel to the opening direction and scrapes the tool as the part is pushed out. Which feature is missing or insufficient?

  2. Resin identification code
  3. A higher cavity count

Show answer and reasoning

Choice 1: draft. A slight release taper reduces contact as the mold opens. Required draft depends on depth, texture, material and tooling.

From Plastic Forming Processes

A sudden thick-to-thin wall change: A housing changes abruptly from a thin wall to a bulky solid region. Which redesign best addresses the geometry problem?

  2. Add a recycling code to the thick region.

Choice 3. A more uniform section and gradual transitions help manage filling and shrinkage. The goal is a manufacturable shape, not merely a larger mass of plastic.

From Choosing a Plastic Forming Process

Parts per hour from four cavities: An ideal molding cycle takes 48 seconds and produces one part in each of four identical cavities. Assume no downtime or rejects. How many parts are produced per hour?

Report to the nearest whole part per hour.

Enter a number, then check it.
Show answer and reasoning

3600 s/h ÷ 48 s/cycle = 75 cycles/h. Then 75 × 4 = 300 parts/h. Reporting 75 ignores the four cavities. Multiplying cycle time by cavity count does not give an hourly rate.

From Choosing a Plastic Forming Process

Tooling cost per part: An illustrative mold costs $7,500 and will make 2,400 acceptable parts with no replacement tooling. What is the tooling cost alone per part? Ignore material and operating costs.

Round to the nearest cent.

Enter a number, then check it.
Show answer and reasoning

$7500 ÷ 2400 = $3.125 per part, or $3.13 per part to the nearest cent. Dividing quantity by tooling cost gives 0.32 parts per dollar, the inverse quantity.

From Choosing a Plastic Forming Process

When two routes cost the same: Two hypothetical routes meet the same specification. A costs $1,200 for tooling plus $9 per part. B costs $13,200 for tooling plus $3 per part. Assume constant variable costs, no scrap and no tooling replacement. At what quantity do total costs match?

Report to the nearest whole part.

Enter a number, then check it.
Show answer and reasoning

Set 1200 + 9N = 13200 + 3N. Thus 6N = 12000, and N = 2,000 parts. Each route then costs $19,200. Using $13,200 without subtracting A's tooling cost gives 2,200, which is wrong.

Choice 1. Deposited roads can carry the main load along the layers. Across-layer tension relies on interlayer bonds. This is a starting choice to test, not a guaranteed strength value.

Count equal-height layers. A simplified print is 30 mm tall. Every layer, including the first, is 0.20 mm thick. How many layers does it have? Give a whole number.

Enter a number, then check it.
Show worked solution

30 mm ÷ 0.20 mm/layer = 150 layers. This assumes constant layer height and says nothing about travel or heating time.

From FDM 3D Printing

Estimate deposited filament mass. Use a simplified volume model: walls and skins total 6 cm³, and the remaining interior is 30 cm³ at 20% infill. Assume a density of 1.24 g/cm³. Ignore supports, purge, brim and other waste. Estimate mass in grams to the nearest 0.1 g.

Enter a number, then check it.
Show worked solution

Deposited volume = 6 + (30 × 0.20) = 12 cm³. Mass = 12 × 1.24 = 14.88 g, or 14.9 g to the nearest 0.1 g. Applying 20% to the entire 36 cm³ would incorrectly reduce the solid walls and give 8.928 g. Real slicer paths need not match this ideal volume model exactly.

Thin, evenly spaced short dashes. Short dashes identify a hidden edge. A center line locates an axis; a visible line shows an edge you can see.

Recognize a visible edge. Which line would you read as an edge directly visible from this viewing direction?

Choose an answer, then check it.

Thick continuous line. A relatively thick continuous line is a visible or object line.

Distinguish an axis from an edge. A thin long–short line passes through the center of a circular hole. What does it identify?

The hole center or axis. The center line locates the hole center or axis. It is not a physical edge.

Recognize an alternate position. A lever outline is repeated in a thin long–short–short pattern beside its solid outline. What is the likely meaning?

Choose an answer, then check it.

Read a dimension line. A thin line has arrowheads at both ends and the value 42 between them. What kind of line is it?

Read an extension line. Thin lines start just outside two part edges and extend to the ends of a dimension line. What are they?

Read section hatching. Thin diagonal strokes fill a region in a section view. What do they ordinarily show?

From Angular Motion

1. Index table in radians: A rotary index table advances 40° between one station and the next. How many radians is one advance?

Enter a number, then check it.
Show worked solution

Put degrees on the bottom so they cancel:

40° × 0.01745329 rad1 ° = 0.6981317… rad

or 0.6981 rad. The same thing exactly: 40° × π/180° = 2π/9 rad. A quick check on the size of the answer — one radian is about 57.3°, so 40° should come out a little under 1 rad, and it does.

From Angular Motion

2. Nameplate speed into the formula: A gearbox output shaft turns at 340 r/min. What is its angular velocity in rad/s?

Enter a number, then check it.
Show worked solution

340 r/min × 0.1047198 rad/s1 r/min = 35.60472… rad/s

or 35.60 rad/s. The factor is not measured, it is the two definitions divided: 2π rad per revolution ÷ 60 s per minute = 0.104719755…

From Angular Motion

3. Spindle slowing down: A spindle is running at 1,800 r/min. The drive brings it down to 600 r/min in 4.0 s. What is its average angular acceleration in rad/s2, taking the running direction as positive?

Enter a number, then check it.
Show worked solution

Only the change in speed matters, so take it first:

Δω = 600 r/min − 1,800 r/min = −1,200 r/min

−1,200 r/min × 0.1047198 rad/s1 r/min = −125.6637 rad/s

Then α = Δω / Δt = −125.6637 rad/s ÷ 4.0 s = −31.4159 rad/s2, or −31.42 rad/s². The sign is the answer as much as the number is: it says the angular acceleration points opposite the direction of rotation, which is what slowing down means. This is the average over the 4.0 s; a drive that ramps its braking has a changing instantaneous value inside the same interval.

From Angular Motion

4. Back to the nameplate: A calculation has produced an angular velocity of 52 rad/s, and the machine has to be set in r/min. What speed is that?

Enter a number, then check it.
Show worked solution

Turn the factor over so that rad/s cancels:

52 rad/s × 9.549297 r/min1 rad/s = 496.5634… r/min

or 497 r/min. Carry the factor to at least five figures — the exact value is 60/(2π) = 9.5492966…, and rounding it to 9.54 puts the answer about 0.1% low, which is a real error on a speed that has to be dialled in.

From Rotation and Linear Speed

5. Belt speed from a drive roller: A conveyor drive roller is 160 mm in diameter and turns at 60 r/min. What is the belt speed in m/s?

Enter a number, then check it.
Show worked solution
  1. Halve the diameter: r = 80 mm = 0.080 m.
  2. Convert the speed: 60 r/min × 0.1047198 rad/s per r/min = 6.283185 rad/s.
  3. v = ωr = 6.283185 rad/s × 0.080 m = 0.5026548 m/s.

The belt runs at 0.503 m/s. Worth a sanity check: 60 r/min is one turn per second, and one turn of a 160 mm roller lays out π × 0.160 m = 0.5027 m of belt — the same number, reached without the formula. The answer assumes the belt does not slip on the roller.

From Rotation and Linear Speed

6. Setting the roller speed: Material has to feed past a station at 1.25 m/s. The drive roller is 250 mm in diameter. What speed must the roller be set to, in r/min?

Enter a number, then check it.
Show worked solution
  1. r = 125 mm = 0.125 m.
  2. Rearrange: ω = v/r = 1.25 m/s ÷ 0.125 m = 10 rad/s.
  3. The machine is set in r/min, so convert back: 10 rad/s × 9.549297 r/min per rad/s = 95.49297 r/min.

Set the roller to 95.5 r/min. Two chances to go wrong here, and both are worth a deliberate check: using 0.250 m instead of the radius halves the answer, and stopping at step 2 leaves it in rad/s, which is not what a drive is dialled in.

From Rotation and Linear Speed

7. Wheel to road speed: A wheel 24 in in diameter turns at 6.0 rad/s. How fast is the vehicle travelling, in mi/h?

Enter a number, then check it.
Show worked solution
  1. r = 12 in, which is exactly 1 ft, or 12 in × 0.0254 m/in = 0.3048 m.
  2. v = ωr = 6.0 rad/s × 0.3048 m = 1.8288 m/s.

Then convert to mi/h:

1.8288 m/s × 1 mi/h0.44704 m/s = 4.0909… mi/h

or 4.09 mi/h. Both factors used here are exact by definition: 1 in = 0.0254 m and 1 mi/h = 0.44704 m/s.

From Rotation and Linear Speed

8. Wheel angular acceleration: A vehicle accelerates at 3.2 m/s2 on wheels 0.62 m in diameter. What is the angular acceleration of one wheel, in rad/s2?

Enter a number, then check it.
Show worked solution
  1. r = 0.31 m.
  2. Rearrange a = αr into α = a/r = 3.2 m/s2 ÷ 0.31 m = 10.3226 rad/s2.

The answer is 10.3 rad/s². Check the unit as well as the number: dividing m/s2 by m leaves 1/s2, and because the radian is a length over a length, rad/s2 is that same thing named for what it describes. The result assumes the wheel rolls without slipping.

From Torque

9. Torque at a pulley: A belt applies 240 N of tangential force to a pulley 300 mm in diameter. What torque does that put on the shaft, in N·m?

Enter a number, then check it.
Show worked solution
  1. The pulley is given by diameter, so halve it: r = 150 mm = 0.150 m.
  2. τ = rF = 0.150 m × 240 N = 36 N·m.

The answer is 36 N·m — lower-case m, because N·M is not a valid SI torque unit; a prefix cannot stand alone. Using the 300 mm diameter instead of the radius gives 72 N·m, exactly twice too much.

From Torque

10. Reading a torque rating: A motor is rated 42 lbf·ft. What is that rating in N·m?

Enter a number, then check it.
Show worked solution

42 lbf·ft × 1.355818 N·m1 lbf·ft = 56.944… N·m

The rating is 56.9 N·m. Read the given unit carefully before reaching for the factor: this motor rating is a torque and converts to the newton metre. This site writes energy as ft·lbf, converting to joules, but word order is only a convention; the quantity and context determine which is meant. The numerical factor happens to be the same 1.355818 either way, so the arithmetic will not warn you if you have read the wrong quantity.

From Torque

11. Force from a torque: A winch drum is 400 mm in diameter and its drive supplies 95 N·m. What tangential force does that produce at the drum surface?

Enter a number, then check it.
Show worked solution
  1. r = 200 mm = 0.200 m.
  2. Rearrange τ = rF into F = τ/r = 95 N·m ÷ 0.200 m = 475 N.

The drive produces 475 N at the drum surface. Notice what the radius is doing: wind more cable onto the drum, the effective radius grows, and the same torque pulls with less force. That single rearrangement is the whole story of a longer wrench, a bigger steering wheel, and a larger pulley.

ω_B = 1500 × 20/50 = 600 rpm. C shares B’s shaft, so ω_C has the same magnitude, 600 rpm. Losses do not change this speed.

Enter a number, then check it.

Stage 1 gives τ_B = 8 × (50/20) × 0.97 = 19.4 lbf·ft. This is the torque available to drive C.

i = 2.5 × 2.5 = 6.25. ω_D = 1500/6.25 = 240 rpm. Do not multiply speed by 0.97².

Enter a number, then check it.

i = 6.25; η_total = 0.97² = 0.9409. τ_out = 8 × 6.25 × 0.9409 = 47.045 lbf·ft. Keep both efficiency factors.
