From Gear Ratios

21. One idler: signed output speed: External gears A22 → I33 → B55 turn from an input of 1100 rpm clockwise. I is an idler. Ignore all losses, including both idler meshes (η = 1.00). Find signed output speed: clockwise positive, viewed from the same end of every shaft. Round to the nearest whole rpm.

Enter a number, then check it.
Show worked solution

The idler count cancels: i = 55/22 = 2.5. Two meshes reverse twice, so output is clockwise: +440 rpm.

Enter 440 rpm.

From Gear Ratios

22. Two idlers: signed output speed: External gears A18 → I30 → J42 → B54 turn from an input of 900 rpm clockwise. I and J are idlers. Ignore all three mesh losses (η = 1.00). Find signed output speed, clockwise positive from the same end of every shaft. Round to the nearest whole rpm.

Enter a number, then check it.
Show worked solution

i = 54/18 = 3. Three external meshes reverse direction three times: output is counterclockwise, so ω_out = −900/3 = −300 rpm.

Enter -300 rpm.

From Gear Ratios

23. Two stages, one idler, three losses: A20 → I30 → B60; B shares a shaft with C24 → D48. I is an idler. Every actual mesh is 95% efficient, including both meshes around I; there are no other losses. What is total efficiency as a percentage? Round to 2 decimal places.

Enter a number, then check it.
Show worked solution

There are two reduction stages but three actual meshes. η_total = 0.95 × 0.95 × 0.95 = 0.857375 = 85.7375%.

Enter 85.74 %.

From Gear Ratios

24. An idler adds a specified mesh loss: A20 → I30 → B60; B shares a shaft with C24 → D48. I is an idler. Input torque is 7 lbf·ft at steady rotation. Every actual mesh is 95% efficient, including both meshes around I; no other losses. Find output torque. Round to 2 decimal places.

Enter a number, then check it.
Show worked solution

i = (60/20) × (48/24) = 6. Three meshes give η_total = 0.95³. τ_out = 7 × 6 × 0.857375 = 36.00975 lbf·ft. The idler adds no reduction factor.

Enter 36.01 lbf·ft.

From Gear Ratios

25. Three stage efficiencies multiply: Three compound reduction stages each have one mesh and are each 96% efficient. There are no idlers or other losses. What is total efficiency as a percentage? Round to 2 decimal places.

Enter a number, then check it.
Show worked solution

η_total = 0.96 × 0.96 × 0.96 = 0.884736 = 88.4736%. Neither 96% nor 288% is the total efficiency.

Enter 88.47 %.

From Gear Ratios

26. Total loss from three efficient stages: Three compound stages each have one mesh and are each 98% efficient. There are no idlers or other losses. What percentage of input power is lost overall? Round to 2 decimal places.

Enter a number, then check it.
Show worked solution

η_total = 0.98³ = 0.941192. Total loss = (1 − 0.941192) × 100 = 5.8808%. Adding three 2% losses gives 6%, which is only an approximation.

Enter 5.88 %.

From Gear Ratios

27. Unequal efficiencies still multiply: Three stages have efficiencies 94%, 97% and 99%, respectively, with one mesh each. There are no idlers or other losses. Find total efficiency as a percentage. Round to 2 decimal places.

Enter a number, then check it.
Show worked solution

η_total = 0.94 × 0.97 × 0.99 = 0.902682 = 90.2682%. Do not average the three percentages.

Enter 90.27 %.

From Gear Ratios

28. Three-stage torque versus ideal torque: A compound train has stage reductions 2:1, 3:1 and 2:1. Input torque is 5 lbf·ft at steady rotation. Each stage has one mesh at 96% efficiency; no idlers or other losses. Find output torque with losses. Round to 2 decimal places.

Enter a number, then check it.
Show worked solution

i = 2 × 3 × 2 = 12. Ideal output torque is 60 lbf·ft; with losses, τ_out = 60 × 0.96³ = 53.08416 lbf·ft.

Enter 53.08 lbf·ft.

From Gear Ratios

29. Three-stage speed stays tied to teeth: A compound train has stage reductions 2:1, 3:1 and 2:1, with input ω_in = 1800 rpm. Each stage has one mesh at 96% efficiency; no idlers or other losses. Find output speed magnitude. Round to 1 decimal place.

Enter a number, then check it.
Show worked solution

i = 12; ω_out = 1800/12 = 150 rpm. Efficiency changes the delivered torque and power, not the positive-drive speed ratio.

Enter 150.0 rpm.

From Gear Ratios

30. Power remaining after three stages: A gear train receives 1600 W. Three stages each have one mesh at 96% efficiency; no idlers or other losses. Find delivered output power. Round to 2 decimal places.

Enter a number, then check it.
Show worked solution

P_out = 1600 × 0.96³ = 1415.5776 W. The stage ratios do not create power.

Enter 1415.58 W.

Keep at least 4 significant figures in η_total: 0.8847 gives 1415.52 W. The absolute tolerance is 0.057600000001 W: the larger of the printed-answer error (0.0024 W) and the 4-significant-figure answer error (0.0576 W), plus 0.000000000001 W to protect the numerical boundary.

From Gear Ratios

31. Work backward through the losses: A two-stage train has overall i = 10:1 and must deliver 80 lbf·ft at steady rotation. Each stage has one mesh at 95% efficiency; no idlers or other losses. What input torque is required? Round to 3 decimal places.

Enter a number, then check it.
Show worked solution

Rearrange τ_out = τ_in × i × η_total: τ_in = 80/(10 × 0.95²) = 8.8642659… lbf·ft. Divide by efficiency when finding the required input.

Enter 8.864 lbf·ft.

From Gear Ratios

32. Minimum stages for a winch: A motor supplies 1920 rpm and 18 lbf·ft. A winch needs at most 40 rpm and at least 800 lbf·ft. Gears may have any integer count from 10–60, with unlimited copies; every reduction stage is at most 6:1 and 97% efficient. No idlers or other losses. Find the minimum feasible number of stages. Enter a whole number.

Enter a number, then check it.
Show worked solution

Speed requires i ≥ 1920/40 = 48. Two stages reach at most 6² = 36, so they fail. Three stages can work: 12 → 48, 15 → 60, 16 → 50 give i = 50, 38.4 rpm and 821.4057 lbf·ft. Thus three stages are sufficient as well as necessary.

Enter 3 stages.

From Gear Ratios

33. Choose a whole-tooth final gear: A winch design uses three compound stages: 12 → 48, 15 → 60, then a 16-tooth driver → an unknown output gear. Choose the final driven tooth count for overall i = 50:1. Available teeth: integers 10–60, unlimited copies; each stage ≤6:1 and 97% efficient, with no idlers or other losses. Enter a whole number.

Enter a number, then check it.
Show worked solution

The first two ratios multiply to 16. The last ratio must be 50/16 = 3.125, so driven teeth = 16 × 3.125 = 50. All teeth are in range and the last stage is below 6:1. Efficiency does not alter the tooth ratio.

Enter 50 teeth.

From Gear Ratios

34. Check the winch speed ceiling: A motor at 1920 rpm drives compound stages 12 → 48, 15 → 60 and 16 → 50 teeth. Each stage is 97% efficient; no idlers or other losses. Find output speed to check a 40 rpm ceiling. Round to 2 decimal places.

Enter a number, then check it.
Show worked solution

i = 4 × 4 × 3.125 = 50. ω_out = 1920/50 = 38.4 rpm, which passes the 40 rpm ceiling. Do not apply efficiency to speed.

Enter 38.40 rpm.

From Gear Ratios

35. Check the winch torque floor: A motor supplies 18 lbf·ft at steady rotation to compound stages 12 → 48, 15 → 60 and 16 → 50 teeth. Each stage is 97% efficient; no idlers or other losses. Find output torque to check an 800 lbf·ft floor. Round to 2 decimal places.

Enter a number, then check it.
Show worked solution

i = 50; η_total = 0.97³ = 0.912673. τ_out = 18 × 50 × 0.912673 = 821.4057 lbf·ft, which passes the 800 lbf·ft floor. Ideal torque alone (900 lbf·ft) is not the check.

Enter 821.41 lbf·ft.

Keep at least 4 significant figures in η_total: 0.9127 gives 821.43 lbf·ft. The absolute tolerance is 0.024300000001 lbf·ft: the larger of the printed-answer error (0.0043 lbf·ft) and the 4-significant-figure answer error (0.0243 lbf·ft), plus 0.000000000001 lbf·ft to protect the numerical boundary.

From Gear Ratios

36. Find the ratio required by torque: For a three-stage winch train, input torque is 18 lbf·ft and required output torque is at least 800 lbf·ft. Each stage has one mesh at 97% efficiency; no idlers or other losses. Find the minimum overall ratio allowed by torque alone; enter X for X:1. Keep at least 4 significant figures in η_total until the final answer. Round to 3 decimal places.

Enter a number, then check it.
Show worked solution

i ≥ 800/(18 × 0.97³) = 48.6970081… . For a 1920 rpm input and 40 rpm ceiling, speed requires only i ≥ 48, so torque is the tighter requirement. Select actual tooth pairs at or above the unrounded bound.

Enter 48.697 for 48.697:1.

Keep at least 4 significant figures in η_total: 800/(18 × 0.9127) = 48.695567… rounds to 48.696. The absolute tolerance is 0.001008068: the larger of the printed-answer error (about 0.000008068) and the 4-significant-figure answer error (about 0.001008068), rounded upward at the numerical boundary. Full precision is preferred and is needed when checking actual tooth choices against the torque floor; 4 significant figures in η_total are accepted for this answer rounded to 3 decimal places.

From Gear Ratios

37. Choose the fastest feasible candidate: A winch needs ≤40 rpm and ≥800 lbf·ft from a 1920 rpm, 18 lbf·ft motor. All three-stage candidates use 10–60 teeth, ≤6:1 per stage and 97% per stage, with no idlers or other losses. A: 12 → 48, 15 → 60, 16 → 48 (48:1). B: 12 → 48, 15 → 60, 16 → 50 (50:1). C: 12 → 36, 10 → 60, 20 → 60 (54:1). Enter X for the X:1 ratio of the fastest candidate that meets both limits. Round to 2 decimal places.

Enter a number, then check it.
Show worked solution

A gives 40 rpm but only 788.549472 lbf·ft: it fails torque. B gives 38.4 rpm and 821.4057 lbf·ft: both pass. C gives 35.5556… rpm and 887.118156 lbf·ft: both pass, but it is slower. Choose B, 50:1. This compares the three supplied candidates, not every possible train.

Enter 50.00 for 50.00:1.

From Saw Blade Selection

Teeth across a quarter inch: A uniform 24 TPI blade crosses 0.250 in of continuous material along the tooth line. Estimate teeth engaged. Give one decimal place.

Enter a number, then check it.
Show worked solution

0.250 in × 24 teeth/in = 6.0 teeth. This is a spacing estimate; actual engagement changes as the blade moves.

From Saw Blade Selection

Teeth across a decimal thickness: A uniform 18 TPI blade crosses 0.250 in of continuous material along the tooth line. Estimate teeth engaged to one decimal place.

Enter a number, then check it.
Show worked solution

0.250 × 18 = 4.5 teeth. Do not divide thickness by TPI; that does not count tooth spacings.

From Saw Blade Selection

Convert thickness before using TPI: A uniform 12 TPI blade crosses 6.35 mm of continuous material. Use 25.4 mm = 1 in. Estimate teeth engaged to one decimal place.

Enter a number, then check it.
Show worked solution

6.35 ÷ 25.4 = 0.250 in. Then 0.250 × 12 = 3.0 teeth. Multiplying millimeters directly by teeth per inch mixes units.

From Saw Blade Selection

Minimum calculated pitch: For 0.125 in of continuous contact, calculate the minimum TPI for an estimated three teeth. Give one decimal place. This asks for the mathematical threshold, not a catalog selection.

Enter a number, then check it.
Show worked solution

3 ÷ 0.125 = 24.0 TPI. Check: 0.125 × 24 = 3 teeth.

From Saw Blade Selection

Select from available pitches: For this simplified exercise, the candidate uniform pitches are 10, 14, and 18 TPI. A continuous contact length is 0.200 in. Which is the coarsest candidate meeting the three-tooth estimate? Enter the TPI. Actual selection also needs the maker's chart.

Enter a number, then check it.
Show worked solution

3 ÷ 0.200 = 15 TPI minimum. The available choice is 18 TPI: 0.200 × 18 = 3.6 teeth. The tempting 14 TPI choice gives only 2.8.

From Saw Blade Selection

Thin-wall tube versus solid bar: A thin-wall tube and a solid bar have the same outside diameter. Which selection approach fits the tube? Enter 1 or 2.
1: Count the whole outside diameter as solid engagement.
2: Use a tube/structural chart with wall thickness and overall size; expect finer teeth than for the solid bar.

Enter a number, then check it.
Show worked solution

2. The hollow center is not material. Engagement changes around the tube, so neither outside diameter alone nor a fixed two-wall sum describes the whole cut.

From Saw Blade Selection

Chip space in soft material: A blade specification calls for widely spaced teeth, generous gullets, and a zero-rake form for chip clearance in a softer material. Which named form fits? Enter 1, 2, or 3.
1: Fine regular.
2: Skip.
3: Positive-rake hook.

Enter a number, then check it.
Show worked solution

2: skip. The generous chip space and zero-rake description identify the form. Final pitch still depends on section size.

From Saw Blade Selection

Identify a positive-rake form: A maker recommends an aggressive positive-rake tooth form for a supported production cut. Which form does that describe? Enter 1, 2, or 3.
1: Regular.
2: Skip.
3: Hook.

Enter a number, then check it.
Show worked solution

3: hook. Positive rake describes the face angle. It does not establish pitch, set, or one universal rake angle.

From Saw Blade Selection

Fine-pitch set for thin sections: For a thin section, a fine-pitch blade specification calls for groups of teeth that gradually change sideways displacement. Which set matches? Enter 1, 2, or 3.
1: Left-right-straight raker.
2: Wavy.
3: Left-right alternate.

Enter a number, then check it.
Show worked solution

2: wavy. Groups create the wave of set. Raker includes an unset tooth; alternate switches sides at each tooth. Set alone does not determine suitable TPI.

From Bench Work with Hand Tools

Hand hacksaw cutting direction: For a conventional push-cut hand hacksaw, which setup is correct? Enter 1 or 2.
1: Teeth away from the handle; pressure on the forward stroke, eased on return.
2: Teeth toward the handle; heavy pressure in both directions.

Enter a number, then check it.
Show worked solution

1. The teeth face the cutting stroke. This describes a conventional hand hacksaw, not a universal power-hacksaw stroke direction.

From Bench Work with Hand Tools

Choose a file for draw filing: A flat face needs light finishing by draw filing after rough shaping. Which is the better starting choice? Enter 1 or 2.
1: A coarse double-cut file chosen for rapid stock removal.
2: A suitable fine single-cut file, kept clean and flat.

Enter a number, then check it.
Show worked solution

2. A fine single-cut file suits controlled draw filing. Keep the file crosswise to the travel and avoid rocking across the face.

From Bench Work with Hand Tools

Choose a file for stock removal: An accessible flat steel edge needs substantial hand shaping before finishing. Which file is the better starting choice? Enter 1 or 2.
1: A suitable bastard-grade double-cut flat file.
2: A fine round file chosen for finishing a small round opening.

Enter a number, then check it.
Show worked solution

1. Match both shape and removal rate. Bastard describes coarseness; double-cut describes the crossing tooth pattern.

From Bench Work with Hand Tools

Respond to chips lodged in a file: A file begins leaving deep scratches, and chips are lodged between its teeth. What should happen next? Enter 1 or 2.
1: Increase pressure so the file forces the chips through.
2: Clear the teeth with a file card, then inspect the work and resume controlled filing.

Enter a number, then check it.
Show worked solution

2. This is pinning. Trapped chips can score the work; extra force does not restore a clean cutting surface.

From Lead Screws

1. Lead: A triple-start screw has pitch 1.5 mm. What is its lead in mm per revolution?

Enter a number, then check it.
Show worked solution

L = pitch × starts = 1.5 × 3 = 4.5 mm/rev. The 1.5 mm spacing is pitch; it is not the travel per turn for this screw.

From Lead Screws

2. Actuator speed: A single-start ACME actuator has 0.20 in pitch and turns at an actual 900 rpm. Its given efficiency is 60%. Find linear speed in in/min during steady engaged travel; the nut cannot rotate.

Enter a number, then check it.
Show worked solution

L = 0.20 × 1 = 0.20 in/rev. Then v = 900 × 0.20 = 180 in/min (3 in/s). Applying 60% to speed would give 108 in/min; efficiency affects force, not the engaged motion ratio.

From Lead Screws

3. Actuator force: A single-start ACME actuator with 0.20 in pitch receives 12 lb-in (lbf·in) of torque. Given overall efficiency 60%, find actual axial force during steady motion against a resisting load. Round to the nearest lbf.

Enter a number, then check it.
Show worked solution

F = 0.60 × 2π × 12 / 0.20 = 226.1947 ≈ 226 lbf. The theoretical force is 376.9911 lbf. Omitting 2π would give only 36 lbf.

From Lead Screws

4. Handle torque: A 120 N hand force acts perpendicular to a vise handle, 180 mm from the screw axis. Find screw input torque in N·m.

Enter a number, then check it.
Show worked solution

From Torque, T = rF = 0.180 × 120 = 21.6 N·m. The supplied 180 mm is already the axis-to-hand radius; do not halve it.

From Lead Screws

5. Clamping estimate: An illustrative single-start square-thread vise has 4 mm pitch and receives 21.6 N·m. Assume a given overall tightening efficiency of 30%, not a measured typical vise value. Estimate force while tightening, in kN, to two decimal places.

Enter a number, then check it.
Show worked solution

L = 0.004 m/rev. F = 0.30 × 2π × 21.6 / 0.004 = 10,178.7602 N = 10.18 kN. Using π = 3.14 gives 10.1736 kN, or 10.17 kN rounded; both are accepted. This is not a rated vise capacity or a residual static-force prediction. Keeping 4 mm beside N·m without conversion makes the result 1,000 times too small.

From Lead Screws

6. Free jaw travel: Before contacting the work, a vise's single-start 4 mm pitch screw turns at 24 rpm. Find jaw speed in mm/s. The nut is restrained from rotation and backlash has been taken up.

Enter a number, then check it.
Show worked solution

v = 24 × 4 = 96 mm/min. Divide by 60: 1.6 mm/s. The jaw cannot keep travelling at that speed through a rigid clamped workpiece.

From Lead Screws

7. Table feed: A CNC positioning slide uses a triple-start screw of 1.5 mm pitch, rotating at an actual 480 rpm. Given efficiency is 55%. Find steady feed in mm/s with the nut restrained from rotating and clearance taken up.

Enter a number, then check it.
Show worked solution

L = 1.5 × 3 = 4.5 mm/rev. v = 480 × 4.5 / 60 = 36 mm/s. Pitch instead of lead gives 12 mm/s; applying efficiency gives 19.8 mm/s; leaving minutes unconverted gives 2,160 with the wrong unit.

From Lead Screws

8. Available thrust: A triple-start screw of 1.5 mm pitch receives 0.75 N·m at steady speed against a resisting load. Given assembly efficiency is 55%. Find actual axial force to the nearest N. This is available screw thrust, before allocating force to guide friction or other loads; it is not a cutting-capacity rating.

Enter a number, then check it.
Show worked solution

L = 1.5 × 3 / 1,000 = 0.0045 m/rev. F = 0.55 × 2π × 0.75 / 0.0045 = 575.9587 ≈ 576 N. Using pitch instead of lead gives 1,727.876 N; omitting 2π gives 91.667 N.

From Lead Screws

9. Required torque: A two-start screw with 2.5 mm pitch must deliver 800 N at steady speed. Its given efficiency is 50%. Find the input torque in N·m, to two decimal places.

Enter a number, then check it.
Show worked solution

L = 2.5 × 2 = 5 mm = 0.005 m. T = FL/(2πη) = 800 × 0.005/(2π × 0.50) = 1.27324 ≈ 1.27 N·m. Divide by efficiency when solving for the required input.

10. Inch coarse callout: What pitch in inches is specified by 1/4-20 UNC? This checked designation appears in NBS Circular 479; the source entry and link are in Screw Threads.

Enter a number, then check it.
Show worked solution

20 is threads per inch: pitch = 1/20 = 0.050 in. The 1/4 is nominal diameter. UNC identifies the coarse series.

11. Inch fine callout: Find the pitch of 1/4-28 UNF in inches, to four decimal places. The NBS Circular 479 designation is checked and linked in Screw Threads.

Enter a number, then check it.

pitch = 1/28 = 0.035714… ≈ 0.0357 in. At the same nominal diameter, the fine series has a smaller pitch than the coarse series.

12. Metric callout: What pitch in mm does M6 × 1.0 specify? The NAAMS standard entry is quoted and linked in Screw Threads.

Enter a number, then check it.
Show worked solution

The pitch is written directly: 1.0 mm. M6 gives the metric family and nominal 6 mm diameter. Do not invert the pitch as though it were a threads-per-inch count.

From Screw Threads

13. One-way thrust: Which form deliberately uses an asymmetric working flank to favor heavy axial thrust in one direction? Choose the form, not a rated capacity: 1 = V, 2 = square, 3 = ACME/trapezoidal, 4 = buttress.

Choose a form, then check it.
Show worked solution

4 — buttress. Its working flank and sloping back are intentionally different. Reverse motion is possible, but heavy loading on the other flank does not keep the same strength and efficiency advantages.

14. Repeated travel: A slide needs a power-screw form suited to repeated travel in both directions, easier machining than square, and a split-nut arrangement to take up wear clearance. Which conventional form best matches? 1 = V, 2 = square, 3 = ACME/trapezoidal, 4 = buttress.

Choose a form, then check it.

3 — ACME/trapezoidal. This trades some square-thread efficiency for practical manufacturing and nut-adjustment advantages. Actual wear life, efficiency and load rating still require assembly data.

From Section Views

Identify a straight complete cut. Which section type uses the straight cut through the entire cylinder shown here?

Choose an answer, then check it.
Show explanation

Full. One straight plane passes through the whole part. Both walls are sectioned.

From Section Views

Identify a quarter removal. Which section type produces this combined exterior and interior view?

Choose an answer, then check it.
Show explanation

Half. Removing one quarter of a symmetric part produces a view with half exterior and half section.

From Section Views

Identify a jogged cut. Which section type follows the jogged path through all three holes?

Choose an answer, then check it.
Show explanation

Offset. The parallel cutting portions are offset to reach staggered holes. The jogs are not edges on the manufactured plate.

From Section Views

Identify a local cutaway. Which section type exposes this passage within an irregular boundary?

Choose an answer, then check it.
Show explanation

Broken-out. A broken-out section removes only a local area to a selected depth in the existing view.

From Section Views

Identify an overlaid slice. The rectangular slice is turned into the drawing plane and placed on the parent bar. What is it?

Choose an answer, then check it.
Show explanation

Revolved section. A revolved section places the rotated cross section on the parent view.

From Section Views

Identify a separate slice. The slice is shown clear of the parent bar and identified by its cut letters. What is it?

Choose an answer, then check it.
Show explanation

Removed section. A removed section is placed apart from the parent view and linked to its location by identification.

From Section Views

Identify a rotated radial cut. One radial cutting portion is rotated into the other before drawing the result. Which section type is used?

Choose an answer, then check it.
Show explanation

Aligned. An aligned section rotates an angled cutting portion into alignment; the top view retains the actual angular locations.

From Section Views

Choose the rib hatch convention. A section plane passes lengthwise through a thin reinforcing rib. Which treatment usually avoids making the rib look like a solid wall?

Choose an answer, then check it.
Show explanation

Leave the lengthwise rib unhatched. A rib cut along its length is conventionally left unhatched; a transverse cut through its thickness is hatched.

From Section Views

Distinguish shaft cut directions. Which statement is appropriate for a solid shaft in an assembly drawing?

Choose an answer, then check it.
Show explanation

A longitudinal shaft is commonly unsectioned; a transverse section can be hatched. The convention depends on cut direction and context. It does not make all shafts immune to sectioning.

From Section Views

Match a cutting plane to its result. Follow the X–X arrows. Which candidate matches the section through this plate?

Choose an answer, then check it.
Show explanation

Result A. Result A. The straight plane crosses the left hole. The right hole lies in the portion removed toward the viewer, so it does not appear in this section.

From Section Views

Interpret the offset jog. The cutting plane jogs across solid material between two holes. Should that jog appear as a new physical edge in the resulting section?

Choose an answer, then check it.
Show explanation

No, the jog changes the imaginary cut path. The offset cutting path is a drawing device, not a step machined into the part.

From Auxiliary and Detail Views

Choose a true-shape view. An inclined face appears as a sloping line in the front view. Which view shows the complete face in true shape?

Choose an answer, then check it.
Show explanation

An auxiliary view looking perpendicular to that face. The projection plane must be parallel to the face. Enlargement does not remove foreshortening.

From Auxiliary and Detail Views

Choose the projector direction. For a primary auxiliary construction, the fold line is parallel to the edge view of the inclined face. How do you draw the projectors?

Choose an answer, then check it.
Show explanation

Perpendicular to the fold line. Projectors are normal to the auxiliary projection plane as represented by its fold line; their direction follows the chosen face.

From Auxiliary and Detail Views

Read a partial auxiliary. A partial auxiliary shows only the sloping face and nearby identifying geometry. What has changed from a complete auxiliary?

Choose an answer, then check it.
Show explanation

The coverage is limited; the projection direction is unchanged. Partial describes which region is shown, not a new projection system.

From Auxiliary and Detail Views

Read a detail scale. A detail is marked 2:1. What does that tell you?

Choose an answer, then check it.
Show explanation

The drawn lengths are twice actual lengths at the intended print scale. A 2:1 view is an enlargement. The actual feature size remains the stated dimension; resized screens or prints are not measuring tools.

From Auxiliary and Detail Views

Read a broken view. A continuous rod is drawn with two break lines and an overall dimension of 360 mm. What is its specified overall length?

Choose an answer, then check it.
Show explanation

360 mm. The dimension gives the full length. The break saves sheet space and does not remove length from the manufactured rod.

Enter a number, then check it.

I = 0.15 A; drop = 0.15 × 80 = 12.00 V. The two drops add to 18 V.

From Series and Parallel Circuits

Parallel supply current. An ideal 18 V DC source supplies parallel 45 Ω and 75 Ω resistors. What is the total supply current? Give three decimal places.

Enter a number, then check it.
Show worked solution

Add branch currents: 0.400 + 0.240 = 0.640 A.

From Series and Parallel Circuits

Parallel equivalent resistance. Find the equivalent resistance of 45 Ω and 75 Ω in parallel. Give two decimal places.

Enter a number, then check it.
Show worked solution

R_eq = (45 × 75) / (45 + 75) = 28.125 Ω, or 28.13 Ω. It is less than either resistor.

From Series and Parallel Circuits

Which series resistor dissipates more?. An ideal 18 V DC source drives 40 Ω and 80 Ω in series. Identify the resistor dissipating more power, then enter that power in watts to two decimal places.

Enter a number, then check it.
Show worked solution

The 80 Ω resistor dissipates more: 0.15² × 80 = 1.80 W. The 40 Ω resistor dissipates 0.90 W.

From Series and Parallel Circuits

Which parallel resistor dissipates more?. An ideal 18 V DC source supplies parallel 45 Ω and 75 Ω resistors. Identify the resistor dissipating more power, then enter that power in watts to two decimal places.

Enter a number, then check it.
Show worked solution

The 45 Ω resistor dissipates more: 18² / 45 = 7.20 W. The 75 Ω resistor dissipates 4.32 W.

From Measuring Electric Circuits

Voltmeter connection and reading. An ideal 18 V DC source drives 56 Ω and 91 Ω in series. Where must an ideal voltmeter connect to read the voltage of the 56 Ω resistor? State the connection, then enter its reading to two decimal places.

Enter a number, then check it.
Show worked solution

Connect across the 56 Ω resistor, in parallel. I = 18 / (56 + 91) = 18 / 147 ≈ 0.1224 A, so the reading is 18 × 56 / 147 ≈ 6.86 V. The numeric checker checks the reading; compare your connection with this explanation.

From Measuring Electric Circuits

Ammeter connection and reading. An ideal 18 V DC source supplies parallel 45 Ω and 75 Ω branches. Where must an ideal ammeter connect to read only the 75 Ω branch current? State the connection, then enter its reading to three decimal places.

Enter a number, then check it.
Show worked solution

Insert it in series within the 75 Ω branch. It reads 18 / 75 = 0.240 A. In the supply lead it would read 0.640 A. The numeric checker checks the reading; compare your connection with this explanation.

From Measuring Electric Circuits

Ohmmeter reads the unpowered network. The source is disconnected and stored energy discharged from a parallel network of 68 Ω and 120 Ω. An ideal ohmmeter is connected across the two network terminals. What does it read? Give two decimal places.

Enter a number, then check it.
Show worked solution

Both paths remain connected. The meter reads their equivalent resistance: (68 × 120) / (68 + 120) = 43.404255… Ω, or 43.40 Ω, not the resistance of either part alone.

From Measuring Electric Circuits

Current from a shunt reading. A voltmeter reads 18 mV across a 0.060 Ω shunt installed in series with a DC load. Find the load current to three decimal places.

Enter a number, then check it.
Show worked solution

18 mV = 0.018 V. I = 0.018 / 0.060 = 0.300 A. The shunt carries the load current; the voltmeter connects across the shunt.

  2. Twist bit

Choose the final-sizing sequence that first establishes references, then controls thickness, width and length. Any preliminary breakdown has already left the blank oversized.

  1. Plane → rip → face-joint → crosscut → edge-joint
  2. Face-joint → edge-joint → plane → rip → crosscut
  3. Crosscut to final length → rip → plane → edge-joint → face-joint

  2. The planer automatically makes one edge square

A curved rail is made from thin strips with grain along their length, bonded together over a form. Which description fits?

  2. Veneering; the face layer alone supplies all support

From How Saws Cut Wood

Count strips with kerf

A board has exactly 12 in of usable width. Each 3 in strip is removed with its own cut from a remaining offcut. Kerf is 0.125 in per cut. Ignore other allowances. What is the maximum whole number of strips?

Enter a number, then check it.
Show answer and reasoning

3 strips. floor(12 / (3 + 0.125)) = 3. Three strips and three kerfs use 9.375 in; four would need 12.5 in. Ignoring kerf gives 4, which does not fit.

From How Saws Cut Wood

Calculate the remaining offcut

From a 10 in usable width, remove three strips, each 2 in wide, using three cuts with a 0.125 in kerf. No other material is removed. What offcut width remains? Enter inches to three decimal places.

Enter a number, then check it.
Show answer and reasoning

3.625 in. 10 − 3(2) − 3(0.125) = 3.625. The kerfs remove 0.375 in. Ignoring them would give 4 in.

From How Saws Cut Wood

Divide a board into equal final strips

An exactly 12 in wide board is divided into four equal strips with three cuts, each with a 0.125 in kerf. Both outside edges are already finished, no offcut remains, and no further allowance is needed. How wide is each strip? Enter inches to three decimal places.

Enter a number, then check it.
Show answer and reasoning

2.906 in to three decimal places. (12 − 3 × 0.125) / 4 = 2.90625 in. Four pieces have three intervening cuts. Ignoring kerf gives 3 in; counting four cuts gives 2.875 in. Both are outside the answer tolerance.

From Geometric Relations in Sketches

Two circles keep one center. The larger circle can change diameter without changing the smaller circle. Which single relation keeps their centers together?

  1. Equal
  2. Concentric
  3. Tangent

Show answer and reasoning

2 — Concentric. It shares the center while leaving the two radii independent. Equal would control size instead.

From Geometric Relations in Sketches

Separated edges on one line. Two nonzero straight edges must stay on the same extended line, with a gap allowed between their ends. What is this geometric relation called?

  1. Parallel
  2. Coincident endpoints
  3. Collinear
Enter a number, then check it.
Show answer and reasoning

3 — Collinear. Parallel alone allows an offset between the lines; coincident endpoints would close the gap. In Onshape, point-on-line constraints can express collinearity.

From Geometric Relations in Sketches

A line touches a round boundary. A straight edge must keep the shown contact with the circle without crossing it. Which relation controls that contact?

  1. Tangent
  2. Equal
  3. Concentric
Enter a number, then check it.
Show answer and reasoning

1 — Tangent. The radius to contact is perpendicular to the line. Equal does not control contact, and concentric applies to centers.

From Geometric Relations in Sketches

A locator point stays halfway. The point must remain halfway between the segment endpoints when the segment grows. Which relation captures that rule?

  1. Coincident with line
  2. Midpoint
  3. Fix
Enter a number, then check it.
Show answer and reasoning

2 — Midpoint. A point merely coincident with the line may slide along it. Fix would hold its current location rather than follow the moving midpoint.

From Geometric Relations in Sketches

Separated arcs share a supporting circle. These two circular arcs must share both center and radius, but their endpoints stay separate. What is the SOLIDWORKS relation name?

  1. Concentric
  2. Equal
  3. Coradial
Enter a number, then check it.
Show answer and reasoning

3 — Coradial. Concentric alone leaves radius free; equal alone leaves center position free. In Onshape, combine concentric and equal radius.

From Geometric Relations in Sketches

Two ribs change length together. Two separate straight segments represent layout ribs. Their lengths must stay equal, while their locations and directions may differ. Which relation should you use?

  1. Equal
  2. Parallel
  3. Collinear
Enter a number, then check it.
Show answer and reasoning

1 — Equal. It links the lengths. Parallel links directions, and collinear puts the segments on the same supporting line.

1 — The free endpoint can move horizontally. The origin coincidence removes two coordinate freedoms and horizontal removes one more from the original four.

From Dimensional Analysis

1. Assembly-line travel time: Two stations are 10 m apart. Parts enter a conveyor 1 ft apart, and the line processes 2 parts every 15 s at a steady rate. How long does one part take to travel from the first station to the second?

Enter a number, then check it.
Show worked solution

The spacing supplies 1 part / 1 ft, and the throughput supplies 15 s / 2 parts. Therefore

10 m × 1 ft0.3048 m × 1 part1 ft × 15 s2 parts = 246.063 s

or 246 s (about 4.10 min). This assumes constant belt speed and steady spacing.

From Dimensional Analysis

2. Recycling-line loading: A recycling conveyor carries 72 lb of material per linear foot. It moves continuously at 0.23 m/s. How many lb of material pass a point in one hour?

Enter a number, then check it.
Show worked solution

Carry the line loading, speed, exact foot factor, and hour conversion together:

0.23 m/s × 1 ft0.3048 m × 72 lb1 ft × 3,600 s1 h = 195,590.551… lb/h

The result is 1.96 × 105 lb/h (about 195,600 lb/h).

From Dimensional Analysis

3. Typing count rate: A typist produces 150 words/min. The average word has 5.1 letters, and one spacebar press follows each word, for 6.1 key presses/word. What is the typist’s key rate in keys/s?

Enter a number, then check it.
Show worked solution

150 words/min × 6.1 keys1 word × 1 min60 s = 15.25 keys/s

Words and minutes cancel, leaving 15.25 keys/s.

From Motion Quantities

4. Average running speed: A runner completes 5 km in 12 min 37 s. What is the runner’s average speed in mi/h?

Enter a number, then check it.
Show worked solution

First convert the distance and time:

5 km × 1 mi1.609344 km = 3.10685596 mi

12 min 37 s = 757 s

Then

3.10685596 mi / 757 s × 3,600 s1 h = 14.775… mi/h

or 14.8 mph.

From Dimensional Analysis

5. Conveyor setting: A packaging conveyor must cover 20 m in 12 s. What speed setting is required in ft/s?

Enter a number, then check it.
Show worked solution

20 m / 12 s × 1 ft0.3048 m = 5.468066… ft/s

The required speed is 5.47 ft/s.

From Dimensional Analysis

6. Reverse exact-factor check: A guard is specified as 18 ft long. What is its length in meters?

Enter a number, then check it.
Show worked solution

Put feet on the bottom so they cancel:

18 ft × 0.3048 m1 ft = 5.4864 m

The exact relationship gives 5.4864 m.

From Measurement Language

7. Prefix scale: A feature is 0.0048 m long. What is its length in mm?

Enter a number, then check it.
Show worked solution

0.0048 m × 1,000 mm1 m = 4.8 mm

The answer is 4.8 mm.

From Geometry, Mass, and Force

8. Squared conversion: A panel has an area of 2.75 ft2. What is its area in in2?

Enter a number, then check it.
Show worked solution

Because 1 ft = 12 in, square the relationship:

2.75 ft2 × 144 in21 ft2 = 2.75 × 144 in2 = 396 in2

The answer is 396 in².

Enter a number, then check it.
Show worked solution

Cube the 12-in-per-foot relationship:

0.50 ft3 × 1,728 in31 ft3 = 0.50 × 1,728 in3 = 864 in3

The answer is 864 in³.

From Acceleration and Squared Time

10. Conveyor acceleration: A conveyor accelerates from rest (0 m/s) to 3 m/s in 5 s. What is its average acceleration?

Enter a number, then check it.
Show worked solution

aavg = (vf − vi) / Δt = (3 m/s − 0 m/s) / 5 s = 0.6 m/s2. The answer is +0.6 m/s² in the selected positive direction.

From Acceleration and Squared Time

11. Direction reversal: Take motion to the right as positive. A cart changes from +2 m/s to −1 m/s in 0.75 s. What is its average acceleration?

Enter a number, then check it.
Show worked solution

aavg = (−1 m/s − (+2 m/s)) / 0.75 s = −3 m/s / 0.75 s = −4 m/s2. The negative sign means the acceleration component points left, opposite the chosen positive direction.

From Dimensional Analysis

12. Complete-part schedule: A cell runs for 7.5 h. Setup takes 20 min, and each repeatable cycle takes 3.6 min per part. How many complete parts fit in the run?

Enter a number, then check it.
Show worked solution

The running window is

7.5 h × 60 min1 h − 20 min = 430 min

Then

430 min × 1 part3.6 min = 119.444… parts

Only 119 complete parts fit; the fraction is time into the next cycle.

From Measurement Language

Practice: A feature is specified as 3,200 µm. What is that length in millimeters?

Enter a number, then check it.
Show worked solution

Micro means 10−6 and milli means 10−3. Moving from micrometers to millimeters divides by 1,000:

3,200 µm × 1 mm1,000 µm = 3.2 mm

From Dimensional Analysis

Practice: A SolidWorks model reports 400 in3. What is the volume in ft3?

Enter a number, then check it.
Show worked solution

There are 12 in in 1 ft, so there are 123 = 1,728 in3 in 1 ft3. Therefore

400 in3 × 1 ft31,728 in3 = 0.23148148 ft3

Rounded sensibly: 0.2315 ft3.

From Motion Quantities

Practice: A cart moves at a constant 4.5 ft/s between two areas 0.25 mi apart. Ignoring loading and turnaround time, what is its idealized round-trip rate per hour?

Enter a number, then check it.
Show worked solution

One round trip is 2 × 0.25 mi = 0.50 mi.

0.50 mi × 5,280 ft1 mi = 2,640 ft

At 4.5 ft/s, one trip takes

2,640 ft / 4.5 ft1 s = 586.667 s

Therefore

3,600 s / 586.667 s = 6.13636

round trips per hour, or about 6.14 round trips per hour. A plan that requires complete trips would schedule 6 and leave time for only part of a seventh.

From Acceleration and Squared Time

Practice: A machine arm starts from rest and reaches 3 m/s in 4 s. What is its average acceleration, assuming the stated interval?

Enter a number, then check it.
Show worked solution

aavg = (vf − vi) / Δt = (3 m/s − 0 m/s) / 4 s = 0.75 m/s2. The assumption is that the requested value is the average over the complete four-second interval.

From Geometry, Mass, and Force

Practice: A sheet-metal enclosure has 1,250 in2 of external surface area. A U.S. gallon of paint covers 350 ft2. Ignoring overspray, waste, unpainted areas, and extra coats, how many complete enclosures can one gallon cover?

Enter a number, then check it.
Show worked solution

Convert the enclosure area using the squared relationship:

1,250 in2 × 1 ft2144 in2 = 8.68056 ft2

Then

350 ft2 / 8.68056 ft2 per enclosure = 40.32 enclosures

Only 40 complete enclosures can be painted. The answer assumes the stated coverage is for the required coat and all paint reaches the enclosure.

From Drying and Conditioning Wood

Moisture from sample masses: A sample initially weighs 144 g. Its oven-dry mass is 120 g. Calculate MC on the oven-dry basis, to one decimal place.

Enter a number, then check it.
Show explanation

Water mass = 144 − 120 = 24 g. MC = 24 / 120 × 100 = 20.0%. Dividing by the initial 144 g gives 16.7%, which is a different basis.

From Drying and Conditioning Wood

Round a moisture result: A sample initially weighs 125 g. Its oven-dry mass is 110 g. Calculate MC on the oven-dry basis, to one decimal place.

Enter a number, then check it.
Show explanation

Water mass = 125 − 110 = 15 g. MC = 15 / 110 × 100 = 13.636…%, or 13.6%. Dividing by the initial 125 g gives 12.0%, which is incorrect for the requested basis.

From Work and Energy

1. Steady lift in SI: A hoist raises a 320 kg load 4.5 m at a steady speed. How much work is done against gravity? Use standard gravity, g0 = 9.80665 m/s2.

Enter a number, then check it.
Show worked solution
  1. The load is a mass, so turn it into the force needed to lift it: F = mg = 320 kg × 9.80665 m/s2 = 3,138.128 N.
  2. W = Fs = 3,138.128 N × 4.5 m = 14,121.576 J.

The work done is 14.1 kJ. Two assumptions are doing real work in that answer: the lift is steady, so no extra force goes into accelerating the load, and the force acts along the direction of travel for the whole 4.5 m.

From Work and Energy

2. A lift in foot pounds-force: How much work is required to lift a 750 lb load 22 ft? Give the answer in joules.

Enter a number, then check it.
Show worked solution
  1. The force needed to lift steadily is the load’s weight, 750 lbf, acting along the 22 ft of travel: W = 750 lbf × 22 ft = 16,500 ft·lbf.

Then convert:

16,500 ft·lbf × 1.355818 J1 ft·lbf = 22,370.997 J

or 22.4 kJ. Note the word order in the working unit: energy is ft·lbf, and it converts to the joule. The 750 lb figure is treated as a weight in pound-force, which is what the formula needs — not a mass in pound-mass.

From Work and Energy

3. A meter reading in megajoules: An electricity meter records 8.4 kW·h over one shift. How many megajoules of energy is that?

Enter a number, then check it.
Show worked solution

A kilowatt hour is a power multiplied by a time and nothing more: one kilowatt sustained for one hour. So 1 kW·h = 1,000 W × 3,600 s = 3,600,000 J exactly, which is 3.6 MJ.

8.4 kW·h × 3.6 MJ1 kW·h = 30.24 MJ

The shift used 30.24 MJ. The kilowatt hour is not itself an SI unit — NIST lists it among the units to be converted into SI — but the factor is exact, so nothing is lost in the conversion.

From Work and Energy

4. Work from a torque: A fastener is run down with a steady 45 N·m through 2.5 revolutions. How much work is done, in joules?

Enter a number, then check it.
Show worked solution
  1. The angle has to be in radians before it can multiply a torque: 2.5 r × 6.283185 rad per r = 15.70796 rad.
  2. W = τθ = 45 N·m × 15.70796 rad = 706.858 J.

The work done is 707 J. Nothing was converted between N·m and J along the way, and nothing needed to be: the radian is a length over a length, value 1, so multiplying by an angle in radians leaves the units alone. Feed the same formula 2.5 revolutions or 900 degrees directly and the answer is wrong, because both of those carry a chosen count inside them.

The steady 45 N·m is an idealization — a real run-down torque climbs as the joint seats.

From Power and Efficiency

5. Horsepower for a lift: A 750 lb load is raised 22 ft in 9 s. How much power does that take, in hp?

Enter a number, then check it.
Show worked solution
  1. W = 750 lbf × 22 ft = 16,500 ft·lbf.
  2. P = W/t = 16,500 ft·lbf ÷ 9 s = 1,833.33 ft·lbf/s.
  3. One horsepower is defined as 550 ft·lbf/s, so dividing by 550 is a unit conversion, not a fudge: 1,833.33 ÷ 550 = 3.3333 hp.

The lift needs 3.33 hp delivered to the load. A motor for the job needs more than that, because no drive is perfectly efficient. Cross-check in SI if you like: 16,500 ft·lbf × 1.355818 = 22,371 J, and 22,371 J ÷ 9 s = 2,486 W, which is 2,486 ÷ 745.6999 = 3.33 hp.

From Power and Efficiency

6. Power from torque and speed: A motor delivers 12 N·m at 1,750 r/min. What is its mechanical power output, in W?

Enter a number, then check it.
Show worked solution
  1. P = τω needs the speed in rad/s: 1,750 r/min × 0.1047198 rad/s per r/min = 183.2596 rad/s.
  2. P = 12 N·m × 183.2596 rad/s = 2,199.1 W.

The output is 2,199 W, or about 2.20 kW. Substituting 1,750 straight into the formula gives 21,000 — wrong by the factor of about 9.55 that separates r/min from rad/s. In coherent SI units the relationship needs no constant at all, which is exactly why the speed has to arrive in rad/s.

From Power and Efficiency

7. The torque-and-rpm shortcut: A drive delivers 250 lbf·in at 1,200 r/min. What is the power, in hp?

Enter a number, then check it.
Show worked solution

The shortcut takes the torque in pound-force inches and the speed in r/min:

hp = (250 lbf·in × 1,200 r/min) ÷ 63,025 = 300,000 ÷ 63,025 = 4.760 hp

The answer is 4.76 hp. Check it the long way, since the constant is only a folded-up set of conversions: 250 lbf·in = 20.833 lbf·ft, 1,200 r/min = 125.664 rad/s, so P = 20.833 × 125.664 = 2,618.0 ft·lbf/s, and 2,618.0 ÷ 550 = 4.760 hp. The two routes agree to four figures.

Give the shortcut a torque in lbf·ft instead and the answer comes out twelve times too small — the constant already contains the inch-to-foot step.

From Power and Efficiency

8. The volts-and-amps shortcut: A direct-current motor draws 14 A at 24 V. What is that electrical input power, in hp?

Enter a number, then check it.
Show worked solution
  1. Electrical power first: P = VI = 24 V × 14 A = 336 W.
  2. Then convert: 336 W ÷ 746 W per hp = 0.4504 hp.

The input is 0.450 hp. The 746 is exact because NIST defines a separate unit, horsepower (electric), as 746 W.

The condition sits in step 1, and this problem satisfies it: volts times amps gives real power in watts on direct current or a purely resistive load. On alternating current it gives apparent power in volt-amperes, and the real power is that multiplied by the power factor — so the same shortcut used on an AC motor without its power factor reads high. This is also the motor’s input; its mechanical output is less.

From Power and Efficiency

9. Hoist efficiency: A hoist motor draws 2.2 kW and raises a 900 N load at a steady 2.0 m/s. What is the efficiency of the system, as a percentage?

Enter a number, then check it.
Show worked solution
  1. Useful output, using P = Fv: 900 N × 2.0 m/s = 1,800 W.
  2. η = Pout/Pin = 1,800 W ÷ 2,200 W = 0.8182.

The system is 81.8% efficient. The ratio is two like quantities, so the watts cancel and the answer is a plain number. The missing 400 W has not vanished — it is heat in the windings, the gearbox, and the bearings. An answer above 100% would mean an error in the numbers, not a remarkable machine.

This is a system efficiency, measured from the electrical input to the load. The motor alone would quote a higher figure, over a different boundary.
